<note>Marbled paper: A decorative paper created by floating oil-based pigments on the surface of water or a thick solution, swirling them into patterns, and then laying a sheet of paper on top to transfer the design. This technique was frequently used for the "endpapers" (the sheets pasted to the inside covers) of high-quality books from the 17th century onward to hide the structural elements of the binding and provide an aesthetic flourish.</note>

<summary>This page consists of a decorative marbled endpaper, representing the traditional craftsmanship and aesthetic choices found in historical bookbinding.</summary>

[This page contains no text.]

<note>Marbled paper: This decorative pattern was created through a process of floating oil-based pigments—in this case, deep red and black—on the surface of a thickened liquid. The artist would swirl the colors into intricate patterns before carefully laying a sheet of paper on top to "print" the design. The addition of gold flecks indicates a high-quality or luxury binding. Historically, these papers were used as "endpapers" to hide the glue and structural components where the book's pages meet the cover, while also providing an elegant visual opening to the work.</note>

<summary>This page features a decorative marbled endpaper with red and black swirls and gold flecks, showcasing the traditional craftsmanship of historical bookbinding.</summary>

# To the Reader

*Judicious Reader,*

There is an abundance of knowledge, yet but little truth is known. The majority of our knowledge is like castles in the air or groundless fantasies. I know of only two ways that are ordained for obtaining wisdom, <term>namely</term> <note>original: "viz." (videlicet)</note> the book of God and the book of Nature; and these also can only be understood if they are read with reason. Many look upon the former as something beneath them and upon the latter as a foundation for atheism, and therefore they neglect both. It is my judgment that just as searching the Scriptures is most necessary, it is also impossible to do so without reason. Faith with-

<summary>In this preface, the translator argues that true wisdom is found only through the "book of God" (Scripture) and the "book of Nature," both of which must be interpreted using reason.</summary>
<keywords>epistemology, reason, Scripture, Nature, John French, wisdom, 17th-century philosophy</keywords>

In this context, it refers to "implicit faith," which is accepting a doctrine without understanding or personal conviction.</note> *If I cannot understand through reason how everything is, I will still seek some reason that a thing is so before I believe it to be so.* I will ground my belief in the <term>Scripture</term> upon reason, and I will improve my reason through <term>Philosophy</term>. How shall we convince those who argue against us <note>original: "gain-sayers"</note> of the truth of the <term>Scriptures</term>, except by using the principles of reason? 

When God made man in his own image, how was that done? It was by making him a rational creature. Therefore, men who set aside reason when reading sacred mysteries only strip away their own humanity <note>original: "un-man themselves"</note> and become further lost in a labyrinth of errors. This is why their religion has degenerated into irrational ideas. 

Now, to say that pure <term>Philosophy</term> is true <term>Divinity</term> <note>original: "Divinity" here refers to theology or the study of the divine.</note> might perhaps be a paradox; yet, if anyone were to claim it, he would not be <term>heterodox</term> <note>meaning: holding opinions that go against established or orthodox religious doctrines.</note>. When <term>Job</term> had spent a long time justifying himself against God—which I believe was because of his ignorance of both God and himself—God undertook to convince him of his error through the principles of <term>Nature</term> and to lead him to the knowledge of both. ### To the Reader.

...at large in **Job 38**. <note>original: "large," completing the phrase "at large," meaning in great detail or at length.</note> Can anyone deny that **Hermes** <note>Hermes Trismegistus, a legendary figure to whom many mystical and alchemical writings were attributed.</note>, **Plato**, and **Aristotle** (even though they were strictly **natural philosophers** <note>original: "Naturalists"; in this era, it referred to those who studied the physical laws of nature.</note>) were not also most profound **theologians**? <note>original: "Divines"</note> Does everyone not grant that the first two chapters of **Genesis** are true **theology**? <note>original: "Divinity"</note> I also dare to affirm that they are the most profound and the truest **philosophy**.

Indeed, they are the foundation and the summary of all **theology** and **philosophy**. If they are rightly understood, they will teach you more knowledge of **God** and yourself than all the other books in the world combined. Now, for a better understanding of them, make use of the most profound *Sendivogius* <note>original: "Sandivogius"; refers to Michael Sendivogius (1566–1636), a famous Polish alchemist and philosopher.</note>, the author of the first of the following **treatises**, as the best **interpreter** <note>original: "Expositor"</note> of them. 

In that treatise of his, you shall see the mystery of the **Deity** and **nature** unfolded, even to the point of wonder. You will see what 그 light and fire is which serves as the throne of **God’s Majesty**; how He is in heaven most gloriously, and in His creatures providentially; and how He is the life of that universal **Spirit** which is spread throughout the whole world. You will learn what that **Spirit** of His is that moved upon the **waters**, and what those **waters** are which are above the **firmament** <note>The "firmament" refers to the vault of the sky as described in the Book of Genesis.</note> and which are under the **firmament**.

The possibility of this is so clearly illustrated in this book by *Sendivogius* <note>original: "Sandivogius"; Michael Sendivogius (1566–1636), a famous Polish alchemist and philosopher.</note> that if any sensible man reads it without bias or prejudice—even just three or four times—he shall, whether he wants to or not <note>original: "nolens volens"</note>, be convinced of its truth. He will also be convinced of many other mysteries just as incredible as this one. 

Therefore, if anyone were to ask me which single book contributes most to the knowledge of God, His creation <note>original: "the Creature"</note>, and their mysteries, I would be speaking against my own better judgment if I did not say *Sendivogius*, second only to the Holy Scriptures <note>original: "sacred Writ"</note>. <header>The Epistle.</header>

there are too many books already; the sheer number of them is the greatest cause of our ignorance, and within them is great vanity. My purpose is instead to let you see the light of Nature, by which you may judge truths and better understand the God of Nature. All natural things are full of Him, and His workings in the way of Nature are most wonderful—enough even to convince the greatest atheists.

*Courteous Reader*, you must excuse me for not striving for elegance <note>original: "affecting elegancies"</note> in these translations; for even if I were skilled in such style, the subject matter of these books would not support it. If I have sometimes used strange <note>original: "uncouth"</note> words, it was because the meaning—to which I remained strictly faithful—would not properly allow for any other, or at least a better word did not occur to me at the time. If any errors <note>original: "Errata's"</note> have slipped through by a slip of my pen or a printer's mistake, please be kind and correct them. If you do not approve of what I have done, prove my error by doing better; for by doing so, you will serve all lovers of truth, and among the rest, your friend,

->*J. F.*<-

# The Preface.

->The author wishes all health to, and prays<-
->to God for a blessing upon, all the search-<-
->ers of alchemy <note>original: "Alchymie"</note>, namely the true Sons<-
->of Hermes <note>A traditional term for alchemists, referring to Hermes Trismegistus, the legendary founder of the "Hermetic" arts.</note>.<-

*Courteous Reader,*

When I considered that many corrupted <note>original: "adulterated"</note> books and false recipes <note>original: "Receipts"</note> of alchemists—composed through the fraud and greed of impostors, and in which not even a single spark of truth appears—were in high demand among the searchers of natural and mysterious arts, by which very many people have been and still are deceived, I thought I could do no better service than to communicate

<summary>The author begins his preface by explaining that he wrote this work to counter the many fraudulent and deceptive alchemical books circulating at the time, which mislead seekers of natural knowledge.</summary>
<keywords>alchemy, Hermes, impostors, natural arts, deceptive books, Michael Sendivogius, recipes</keywords>

<header>The Preface.</header>

...that talent, committed to my trust by the **Father of Lights** <note>original: "Father of Lights" — a biblical reference to God as the source of all enlightenment (James 1:17).</note>, to the **Sons** and **Heirs** of **Wisdom** <note>A traditional term for those initiated into the secrets of alchemy.</note>. And for this purpose: that future ages may take notice that this singular **philosophical** blessing of **God** has not been denied to some men—not only in former ages, but also in this one. It seemed right to me, for certain **reasons**, to conceal my name; I do not seek praise for myself, but endeavor to be helpful to the lovers of **Wisdom**. Therefore, I leave that vain desire for honor to those who would rather seem to be wise than to be so in reality. **What** I write here as a testimony to that undoubted **philosophical** truth, expressed in these few lines, has been taken from that **manual** experience <term>practical, hands-on laboratory work</term> which the most **High** has granted to me. I have done this so that those who have laid the principal and real foundations in this commendable **Art** <note>original: "Art" — referring to the "Great Art" of alchemy.</note> may, by this...

<header>The Preface.</header>

...encouragement not to forsake the practice of the best things, and so be secured from that wicked swarm of smoke-sellers <note>original: "smoke-sellers" (Latin: *fumivenduli*) — a term for charlatans who sell worthless or deceptive promises, particularly fraudulent alchemists.</note>, whose delight is to cheat. They are not dreams, as the ignorant common people call them; neither are they the foolish inventions of idle men, as fools and men lacking understanding (who mock the <term>Art</term> <note>The "Art" refers to the "Great Art" of alchemy—the study of transmuting base metals and seeking the Elixir of Life.</note>) imagine them to be. 

*It is the philosophical truth itself, which—as I am a lover of the truth—I ought not, indeed I could not, keep hidden or bury in silence, so that I may support and confirm the truth of* <term>Alchemy</term> <note>original: "Alchymie"</note>*, which is so undeservedly denounced.* 

Although this truth might be very fearful in these times (when virtue and vice are held in equal regard) to come forth upon the public stage of the world, because of the worthlessness of this age and the ingratitude and treachery of men (to say nothing of the warnings of the *Philosophers* <note>original: "curses of Philosophers" — traditional alchemical texts often included "curses" or dire warnings against those who revealed secrets to the "profane" or unworthy.</note>). *I* could produce witnesses

### *Of Nature: what she is, and what those who search for her ought to be.*

**M**any wise and very learned men from many ages ago—indeed (as Hermes <note>original: "Hermes"; likely referring to Hermes Trismegistus, the legendary Hellenistic figure considered the father of alchemy</note> testifies) even from before the Great Flood—wrote many things concerning the creation of the <term>Philosopher’s Stone</term> <note>original: "Philosophers stone"; a legendary alchemical substance capable of turning base metals into gold or providing an elixir of life</note>. # THE THIRD TREATISE.
## *Of the true first matter of Metals.*

---

The first matter of metals is twofold, but one cannot create a metal without the other. The first and most important is the humidity of the air mixed with heat; this is what the philosophers called *Mercury*, which is governed by the beams of the Sun and Moon in the *philosophical sea*. The second is the dry heat of the earth, which they called *Sulphur*. 

Because all true philosophers have primarily hidden this fact, we will explain it a bit more clearly—especially regarding the weight or <term>poise</term> <note>original: "poise"; this refers to the precise balance or proportional weight of the ingredients.</note>. If this weight is unknown, the entire work is ruined. The entire grain or body is not turned into seed; instead, only a "spark," or a small, essential part within the body becomes the seed. # THE FOURTH TREATISE.

## *How Metals are generated in the bowels of*
## *the earth.*

Metals are produced in this manner: After the four Elements have sent their powers <note>original: "vertues"; in this context, it refers to the essential properties or qualities of the elements.</note> into the center of the earth, the <term>Archeus</term> <note>In alchemy and early medicine, the Archeus was the vital internal force or "master workman" that directed natural processes.</note>, by way of distillation, sends them up to the <term>superficies</term> <note>original: "superficies"; the surface or outermost layer.</note> of the earth, driven by the heat of its perpetual motion. For the earth is porous, and this "wind," by distilling through the pores of the earth, is resolved into water, out of which all things are made. 

Therefore, let the "sons of wisdom" <note>A traditional term for students or practitioners of alchemy.</note> know that the seed <note>original: "sperm"; refers to the generative essence or life-force.</note> of metals does not differ from the seed of all things—namely <note>original: "viz."; an abbreviation for the Latin *videlicet*, meaning "namely" or "that is to say."</note>, the moist vapor. ## THE FIFTH TREATISE.

### *On the Generation of All Kinds of Stones.*

The material of stones is the same as that of other things; and they are formed according to the purity of their locations in this manner. When the four Elements <note>Earth, Air, Fire, and Water.</note> distill their vapor into the center of the earth, the <term>Archeus</term> <note>In alchemical philosophy, the Archeus is the "master chemist" or vital force of nature that directs the formation and growth of minerals and living things.</note> of nature sends that vapor forth and refines it through heat. 

As this vapor passes through different areas and the pores of the earth, it carries along all the impurity of the earth up to the very surface <note>original: "superficies"</note>. Afterward, the air solidifies <note>original: "congeals"</note> it. (For what the pure air creates, the heavy <note>original: "crude"</note> air solidifies, because air has entrance into air and they join together, for nature delights in its own nature <note>original: *natura natura laetatur*</note>.) 

In this way, rocks and stony mountains are created, shaped by the size of the earth's pores. The larger the pores of the earth, the better that place is purified. Since a greater amount of heat and water passes through such a "breathing place" or vent, the earth is <term>cleansed</term> <note>original: "depurated"</note> more quickly. Consequently, in those locations, metals are more easily produced afterward.

Afterward, they join them together again, not realizing that a man is not created from a human body cut into pieces; by doing this, the body is ruined and the seed is destroyed beforehand. 

Everything is multiplied through <term>male</term> and <term>female</term> principles, as I have already mentioned in the treatise on the twofold <term>Matter</term>. The separation of the sexes produces nothing on its own; only a proper joining of them together brings forth a new form. Therefore, the seeds—or <term>sperms</term>—must be used, not the bodies themselves. 

Therefore, take a living <term>male</term> and a living <term>female</term>; join these together so that a <term>sperm</term> may be conceived between them to produce fruit according to its kind. No living person can believe that he can create the <term>first matter</term>. The <term>first matter</term> of <term>man</term> is earth, and no one can make a human being out of that; only God knows how to do this. However, from the <term>second matter</term> (which is already prepared), if it is placed in its proper environment, a thing of the same <term>species</term> or kind as the seed may easily be generated through the operation of <term>Nature</term>. 

In this process, the <term>artist</term> needs to do nothing except separate the thin from the thick, and put it into its proper <meta>The text continues on the next page with the word "vessel."</meta>

# THE SEVENTH TREATISE.

### *On the power of the second matter.*

**B**UT so that you may more easily understand <note>original: "conceive"</note> what this second matter is, I will describe its powers <note>original: "vertues"</note>, by which you may recognize it. First of all, know that Nature is divided into three Kingdoms. Two of them are such that either could exist by itself, even if the other two did not: these are the Mineral, Vegetable, and Animal Kingdoms. The Mineral Kingdom can exist on its own, even if there were no man in the world, nor any tree or herb. Likewise, the Vegetable Kingdom can stand by itself, even if there were no metal or animal. These two are made of one thing, by one cause. But the third—the Animal Kingdom—derives its life from <margin>*</margin> the other two which we have mentioned; without them, it could not exist. It is more noble and excellent than those two, and it is also the last of the three and rules over the others. This is because power <note>original: "vertue"</note> or excellence always reaches its completion in a third thing, and is multiplied in the second.

# THE NINTH TREATISE.

### *On the Mixing of Metals, or the extraction of their seed.*

We have spoken about nature, art, the body, sperm, and seed; now let us proceed to <term>practice</term> <note>original: "Praxis," meaning the practical application or action of a craft</note>—namely, how metals ought to be mixed together and what their correspondence or agreement is with one another. 

Know, therefore, that a woman does not differ essentially from a man; both are bred from the same seed and in one <term>womb</term> <note>original: "Matrix"</note>. The only difference was in the digestion <note>in alchemy, "digestion" refers to the process of maturation through heat</note>, and the fact that the womb contained purer blood and salt. In the same way, silver is made of the same seed as gold and in the same womb, but the womb contained more water than digested blood, according to the phase of the Moon in the heavens. 

But so that you may more easily imagine how metals couple together—so that their seed may be released and received—look at the heavens and the planetary spheres. You see that Saturn is placed the highest; next to that is Jupiter, then Mars, then *Sol* <note>the Sun</note>, then Venus, then Mercury, and last of all *Luna* <note>the Moon</note>. Consider also that the powers <note>original: "vertues"</note> of the planets do not ascend, but descend. Experience teaches us as much: for instance, iron (*Mars*) is not made from copper (*Venus*), but...

If, therefore, you intend to apply your mind to create things, first consider those things that are already made. ...eyes of the wise look upon Nature differently than the eyes of common men. That internal <note>original: "intrinsecall"</note> heat is far more effective than this ordinary <note>original: "Elementary"</note> fire; but it is tempered with an earthy water, which day by day penetrates the pores of the earth and cools it. In the same way, the air tempers and mitigates the heavenly Sun and its heat, for this air flies around the world day after day. Unless this were so, all things would be consumed by such great heat, and nothing would be produced. For just as that invisible fire, or central heat, would consume all things if the water coming between them did not prevent it, so the heat of the Sun would destroy all things if the air did not come between them. 

But I will briefly explain how these <term>elements</term> <note>The four classical elements: Earth, Water, Air, and Fire</note> work with one another. That heat creates air in this manner: the <term>matrix</term> <note>original: "Matrix"; the source, womb, or medium in which something is formed</note> of air is water, which brings forth offspring of its own nature, but which are different and far more subtle than itself.

# THE
# EPILOGUE, or CONCLUSION
### OF THESE
# TWELVE TREATISES.

->FRIENDLY READER,<-

I wrote the twelve foregoing treatises out of love for the sons of Art <note>original: "sonnes of Art"; a traditional term for alchemists or practitioners of the hermetic sciences</note>, so that before they set their hands to the work, they may know the operation of Nature—namely <note>original: "viz."</note>, how she produces things through her working. This is so they do not attempt to enter at the gate without keys, or to draw water in a sieve; for he labors in vain who puts forth his hands to work without the knowledge of Nature. In this sacred and most true Art, he lies in nocturnal darkness to whom the sun does not shine, and he is in thick darkness to whom the moon does not appear after nightfall. 

Nature has her own proper light, which is not obvious to our eyes; the shadow of Nature is a body before our eyes. But if the light of Nature enlightens anyone, the cloud is immediately <note>original: "presently"</note> taken away from before his eyes, and without any hindrance <note>original: "let"</note> he can behold the point of our lodestone <term>lodestone</term> <note>A naturally magnetized mineral, used here as a metaphor for the guiding principle or point of attraction in alchemical work</note>, which corresponds to each center of the rays—namely, of the Sun and Earth. For so far...

reason that encouraged me to make it so plain was this: namely <note>original: "viz."</note>, because when I had talked with many men who thought they understood the writings of the Philosophers very well, I perceived that they explained those writings far more subtly than Nature—which is simple and plain—required. ## A TREATISE
-> OF <-
# SULPHUR:
### *The Preface.*

**COURTEOUS READER,**

Seeing I might not write more clearly than other ancient philosophers have written, perhaps you may not be satisfied with my writings—especially since you already have so many other books by philosophers in your hands. But believe me, I have no need to write books because I seek neither profit nor <term>vain glory</term> <note>original: "vain glory"; excessive pride in one's own achievements or seeking empty praise</note> through them; therefore, I do not reveal who I am. Those things which I have now published for your profit and advantage seem to me to be more than enough. I intend that other things which remain shall be referred to the *Book of Harmony*, where I have extensively treated natural things. Yet, by the persuasion of some friends, I must also write this *Treatise of Sulphur*; in which whether it be necessary to add any <meta>catchword: thing</meta>

For if you would consider with mature judgment how Nature works, you would have no need for so many volumes by philosophers; in my opinion, it is better to learn from Nature the mistress than from her students. 

You have enough in the preface of the book of the *Twelve Treatises*, as well as in the first treatise itself. In this Art <note>The alchemical art of transmutation</note>, there are so many massive books to be found that they hinder rather than help those who study it. If in any science or art it helps or hurts much to have one word missing or added, then it is even more so in this one. My advice is that you persist in the text, and whatever you read, apply it to the possibilities of Nature. In the first place, inquire diligently into what Nature is. 

All authors indeed write that she is a thing of small account, easy, and common; and indeed it is true, but it should have been added that she is so only to wise men. The wise man knows her to be among dung, while the ignorant man does not believe her to be in gold. And all these men who have written such difficult books—if they were now ignorant of the Art <note>The alchemical art of transmutation.</note> and had to find it out from such books (which are indeed very true)—they would find it with more difficulty than the men who search into the art today. 

I will not praise my own writings; he who applies them to the possibilities and course of Nature shall judge them. # OF
# SULPHUR:
## *The Second Principle.*

Sulphur is not the least <note>original: "last," used here to mean least important or lowest in rank.</note> among the principles because it is a part of metal—indeed, it is the principal part of the Philosophers' Stone. Many wise men have left various and very true writings about sulphur. Even Geber <note>Jabir ibn Hayyan (c. 721–c. 813), a foundational figure in alchemy whose Latinized works were central to European science.</note> himself, in the 28th chapter of his first book, *The Sum of Perfection* <note>original: "highest perfection." This refers to the *Summa perfectionis magisterii*, one of the most important medieval alchemical texts.</note>, says: "By the grace of the Most High God, it illuminates every body, because it is light from light, and a tincture." <note>In alchemy, a "tincture" is a potent substance capable of infusing its properties or color into another material, often used as a synonym for the Elixir or the Stone.</note>

But before we treat it, it seems good to first describe the origin of the principles, especially since sulphur has long been considered the chief among them. Until now, very few have shown where these principles arise from; and it is difficult to judge any principle—or anything else—whose origin and generation is unknown. After all, what can a blind man judge of color? What our predecessors have omitted, we intend to provide in this treatise.

Now, the principles of things—especially of metals—are two according to the ancient philosophers: sulphur and mercury. However, according to more recent <note>original: "latter"</note> philosophers, there are three: salt <note>original: "Sal"</note>, sulphur, and mercury. The origin of these principles lies in the four elements, and we will begin by explaining their origin first.

Therefore, let students of this sacred science know that there are four elements, and that each of these four has another element at its center by which it is "elementated" <note>This archaic term implies that each element's internal nature or "soul" is defined by the essence of another element acting upon it from within.</note>. These are the four pillars <note>original: "statues"</note> of the world, separated from Chaos during the creation of the world by divine wisdom. These uphold the fabric of the world through their opposing actions—balanced in equality and proportion—and, through the influence of heavenly powers <note>original: "inclination of celestial virtues"</note>, they bring forth everything that exists within and upon the earth. We will discuss these in their proper places; for now, let us return to our purpose and begin with the nearest element: namely <note>original: "viz." (videlicet)</note>, the Earth.

### ABOUT
# THE ELEMENT OF THE
# EARTH.

**T**HE Earth is of great worth in its quality and importance <note>original: "dignity"</note>. In this element, the other three—especially fire—rest. It is the most excellent element for concealing and discovering those things which are entrusted to it. It is dense <note>original: "grosse"</note> and porous; it is heavy in respect to its mass <note>original: "small-nesse"; here referring to its density or bulk</note>, but light in respect to its nature. It is also the center of the world, as well as the center of the other elements. The axle tree <note>The *axis mundi*, or the imaginary line on which the Earth and heavens were thought to rotate.</note> of the world and of both poles passes through its center.

It is porous, as we said, like a <term>sponge</term>, and brings forth nothing of its own accord. Instead, it receives everything that the other three elements distill and project into it; it keeps all things that are to be kept and brings to light all things that are to be brought to light. It produces (as we said before) nothing from itself, but it is the receptacle of other things. It is that in which everything that is brought forth remains; by the heat of motion, everything is broken down <note>original: "putrefied"</note> within it and is multiplied by that same motion, as the pure is separated from the impure. 

That which is heavy is hidden within it, and the heat drives that which is light up to its <term>surface</term> <note>original: "superficies"</note>. After they have entered, they break forth again through the axle-tree of the Antarctic pole. Because the air does not allow for an imbalance <note>original: "inequality"; here meaning a vacuum or a lack of uniformity in pressure</note>, the waters are forced to return to the Arctic pole, their center, and so they continually follow this cycle. 

In this journey from the Arctic pole to the Antarctic pole through the middle—or the axle-tree of the world—the waters are dispersed through the pores of the earth. Depending on the volume <note>original: "more or lesse"</note>, springs arise; these later meet together and grow to become rivers, eventually returning to the place from which they first emerged. This process is done incessantly through the **universal motion** <note>the perpetual movement of the heavens and elements that alchemists believed powered all natural processes</note>. 

Some people (as I mentioned before), being ignorant of this universal motion and the operations of the poles, say that these waters are consumed in the heart of the sea and then generated by the stars. However, the stars produce and generate no material thing; they only impress "virtues" <note>inherent natural powers or qualities</note> and spiritual influences, which cannot give any physical weight to things. Therefore, waters are not generated from nothing; instead, know that they come forth from the center of the sea, through the pores of the earth, and into the whole world. 

From these natural conclusions or principles, <term>philosophers</term> <note>original: "Philosophers"; in this era, the term referred to "natural philosophers," the predecessors of modern scientists</note> have invented various instruments and ways to transport water, as well as fountains, since it is known that water cannot naturally rise higher than its source...

Therefore, let the **searcher** of this sacred science know that the soul in man—the lesser world or **microcosm**—taking the place of its **center**, is the **King**. It is placed in the vital spirit, in the purest blood. The soul governs the mind, and the mind governs the body. When the soul conceives anything, the mind knows all things, and all the limbs understand the mind, obey the mind, and desire to fulfill its will. 

For the body knows nothing; whatever strength or motion is in the body is caused by the mind. The body is to the mind as instruments are to the **artisan** <note>original: "Artificer"</note>. Now the soul, by which man differs from other **animals**, operates within the body, but it has a greater operation outside of the body, because outside the body it reigns absolutely. Through this wisdom, He works outside of the world and conceives much higher things than the physical world is able to understand; these things are beyond Nature, being the secrets of God alone. 

You have the soul as an example: it can imagine many profound things while being distinct from the body. In this, the soul is like God, who works beyond Nature from outside the world. However, the soul compared to God is like a candle lit against the light of the midday sun. The soul imagines but cannot execute its thoughts except within the mind; but God brings all things into being at the very moment He imagines them. For instance, the soul might imagine something being done in *Rome* or elsewhere in the blink of an eye, but only within the mind. But God, who is omnipotent, does all such things in reality <note>original: "essentially"</note>. 

Therefore, God is not contained within the world, except in the way the soul is in the body. He has His absolute power separate from the world, just as the soul of any person has its absolute power separate from the body to do things the body cannot conceive. The soul, therefore, has great power over the body if it so chooses—otherwise, our philosophy would be pointless. 

By these examples, therefore, learn to know God, and you shall understand how the Creator differs from the created being <note>original: "Creature"</note>. You yourself will be able to conceive greater things now that we have opened the gate for you. But so this treatise does not grow too large, let us return to our main purpose.

Thus they rise and increase until the Earth can rise no higher with them. In the meantime, those two elements are <term>refined</term> <note>original: "subtilized"; in alchemy, the process of making a substance more spiritual, pure, or volatile (gas-like).</note> by being held within the Earth. From this refinement come flowers and fruit, in which the elements become "friends," as you may see in trees. For the more they are refined and purified by rising, the better the fruit they produce, especially if they finish with their powers equally joined together.

## CONCERNING

# SULPHUR:

**THE** philosophers have not undeservedly placed Sulphur in the first place among the three principles <note>The "Three Principles" (Tria Prima) of Paracelsian alchemy are Sulphur, Mercury, and Salt, believed to be the base components of all metals.</note>, as it is the most worthy principle, in the knowledge of which the whole Art consists. Now, there is a threefold Sulphur, and one must be chosen above the rest: a Sulphur for tinting <note>original: "tinging"; the process of changing the color and quality of a metal, usually toward gold or silver.</note> or coloring; a Sulphur for congealing Mercury; and the third is essential and ripening. 

We ought to treat these seriously; but because we have presented one of the principles by way of a dialogue, we shall also conclude the rest in the same manner, lest we should seem to be partial and detract from either of them. Sulphur is more mature than any of the other principles, and Mercury is not coagulated <note>thickened or solidified from a liquid state</note> except by Sulphur. Therefore, our whole operation in this Art is nothing else but to know how to draw forth that Sulphur out of metals, by which our <term>Argent vive</term> <note>original: "Argent vive"; literally "living silver," the archaic term for Mercury or quicksilver.</note> in the bowels of the Earth is congealed into gold and silver.

## THE
# CONCLUSION

Every seeker of this Art must, first and foremost, examine with mature judgment the creation, operation, and virtues of the four <term>Elements</term> <note>Earth, Air, Fire, and Water—the fundamental building blocks of matter in pre-modern science.</note>, together with their actions. For if he is ignorant of their origin and nature, he will not come to the knowledge of the Principles; nor will he know the true matter of the <term>Stone</term> <note>The Philosopher's Stone, the ultimate goal of alchemy, capable of transmuting metals and perfecting the human soul.</note>, much less reach any successful conclusion. This is because every end is rooted in its beginning: he who understands his beginning well will understand what the end shall be. 

For the origin of the Elements is <term>Chaos</term> <note>The primary, unformed state of matter from which the universe was created; in alchemy, it often refers to the "First Matter" (Materia Prima).</note>, out of which God, the Creator of all things, created and separated the Elements—an act which belongs to God alone. But from the Elements, Nature produces the <term>Principles</term> <note>In alchemical theory, these are the Three Principles: Salt, Sulfur, and Mercury, which combine to form all physical substances.</note> of things, and this is Nature's work, through the will

...of God alone. Out of the Principles, <term>Nature</term> afterwards produces minerals and all things; out of these, the <term>Artist</term> <note>The alchemist or practitioner of the chemical arts.</note>, by imitating <term>Nature</term>, can also do many wonderful things. Because <term>Nature</term> produces minerals, metals, and all kinds of things from these Principles—which are <term>Salt</term>, <term>Sulphur</term>, and <term>Mercury</term>—and because it does not simply produce metals directly from the Elements, but through Principles which act as the medium between the Elements and metals; therefore, if <term>Nature</term> does not create those things [directly from the Elements], much less shall Art.

And not only in this example, but also in every natural process, a middle state <note>original: "disposition"—the arrangement or transitional stage of matter.</note> is to be observed. Therefore, in this treatise, we have sufficiently described the Elements, their actions, and operations, as well as the origin of the Principles (because until now, no philosopher has revealed these things more clearly). This was done so that the well-intentioned seeker might more easily consider to what degree the <term>Stone</term> <note>The Philosopher's Stone.</note> differs from metals, and metals from Elements. 

For there is a difference between gold and water, but less of a difference between water and mercury, and the least difference of all between mercury and gold. For the house <note>The source or "home" where a substance is naturally contained or generated.</note> of gold is mercury, and the house of mercury is water. But <term>Sulphur</term> is that which coagulates <note>Hardens or solidifies from a liquid state.</note> mercury. This <term>Sulphur</term> is indeed very difficult to prepare, but even more difficult to find. For this secret consists in the "Sulfur of the Philosophers," which is also contained in the inner rooms of mercury. We shall discuss the preparation of mercury (without which it is useless) later in the section on the third Principle, Salt, since here we are treating the virtue and origin of <term>Sulphur</term>, not its practical application <note>original: "Praxis"—the actual lab work and procedures.</note>.

Therefore, we have not written this treatise because we want to disprove any of the ancient philosophers, but rather to confirm their writings and supply those things which they omitted. Since philosophers themselves were only human, they could not be accurate in everything; nor is one man sufficient for all things. Miracles have also led some men away from the true path of Nature, as we read happened to *Albertus Magnus* <note>A 13th-century German philosopher and theologian who wrote extensively on the natural sciences and alchemy.</note>, a very clever <note>original: "witty"—in this context, meaning intellectually sharp or ingenious.</note> philosopher. He wrote that in his time, grains of gold were found between the teeth of a dead man in his grave. He could not explain this miracle, but judged it to be because of the "mineral virtue" <note>The inherent power or property within a substance that causes it to act according to its nature.</note> in man. He was confirmed in his opinion by that saying of *Morien* <note>A legendary alchemist often cited as the teacher of King Khalid ibn Yazid.</note>: "*And this matter, O King, is extracted from you.*" <note>original: "Et haec res, o Rex, ex te extrahitur"—a famous alchemical maxim suggesting the source of the Philosopher's Stone is found within the human microcosm.</note> However, this is an error, for *Morien* intended those things to be understood philosophically.

For the mineral virtue is placed in its own kingdom, just as the animal virtue is in its own kingdom. As in the book of the *Twelve Treatises*, we have distinguished those kingdoms and divided them into three: the animal, vegetable, and mineral kingdoms. Each of these stands on its own and multiplies without the entrance <note>original: "ingresse"—the act of entering or combining with an external substance.</note> of any other thing. It is true indeed that in the animal kingdom, <term>Mercury</term> <note>In alchemical theory, Mercury is the fluid, passive principle of matter.</note> is like the matter, and <term>Sulphur</term> <note>In alchemy, Sulphur is the active, formative, or "soulic" principle.</note> is like the virtue, but the animal is not mineral. If the virtue of the animal <term>Sulphur</term> were not in man, it could not congeal the blood (<term>Mercury</term>) into flesh and bones. Similarly, if there were not a virtue of the vegetable <term>Sulphur</term> in the vegetable kingdom, it could not coagulate water (the vegetable <term>Mercury</term>) into herbs and trees. The same is to be understood in the mineral kingdom. These three Mercuries do not actually differ

It is enough for the diligent student that he has heard here what the origin of the <term>Principles</term> <note>In alchemy, these are Salt, Sulphur, and Mercury—the fundamental building blocks of all matter.</note> is. Since if the beginning is unknown, the outcome is always doubtful. In this <term>treatise</term> <note>original: "Treatise"</note>, we have spoken of these matters to the seeker not cryptically <note>original: "Ænigmatically"—referring to the traditional alchemical practice of hiding secrets behind riddles or symbols.</note>, but as clearly as we could and as much as was permitted to us. By these means, if God enlightens anyone’s mind, he shall know what a successor owes to those who came before him, seeing as this <term>Art</term> <note>Alchemy was frequently referred to as "The Art" or the "Hermetic Art."</note> is always acquired by the same kind of intellects <note>original: "wits"</note> and temperaments <note>original: "dispositions"</note>. After this clear manifestation of the Art, we place it into the care <note>original: "bosome"</note> of God, the most high Creator and our Lord. We commend ourselves, together with all honest-hearted readers, to his grace and infinite mercy. To whom be praise and glory, forever and ever.

<header>A true Light of Alchemy.</header>

# A true Light of Alchemy.

Many such mishaps and accidents occur, which, when not well considered by writers, cause readers to fall into error. Yet the honest practitioner must apply all things to the possibilities of Nature; for if they do not agree with Nature, they must be left alone and set aside <note>original: "waved"</note>.

But for you, Christian reader, who here briefly sees the whole council of the <term>Principles</term> <note>In alchemy, these are the three fundamental components of matter: Salt, Sulphur, and Mercury.</note> (since the beginning is known, the end is always doubtful), we have spoken of these in this treatise not casually, but as clearly as we could and as much as was permitted <note>original: "lawfull"</note> to us. By these means, if God shall enlighten your understanding, you shall know what it means to follow others. Seeing as this <term>Art</term> <note>The "Hermetic Art" or Alchemy.</note> is always justified by its own "sons"—the wise and those deep in the Art which they know—dedicate this manifestation of it to the honor of God the most high Creator and our Lord. We commend ourselves, together with all true and humble keepers of his commandments, to him for his help and glory, forever and ever, AMEN.

### *Of the generation of Natural things.*

<margin>The generation of natural things is twofold.</margin>
<margin>All things proceed from putrefaction.</margin>
**T**he generation of all natural things is twofold: natural, occurring without human skill <note>original: "without Art"</note>; and artificial, namely, by alchemy <note>original: "Alchymie"</note>. Although in general it may be said that all things are naturally generated from the earth by means of putrefaction <note>In early modern science, putrefaction was not merely rotting, but a transformative process of breakdown and fermentation believed to be necessary to release the "seed" or essence of a new thing.</note>. For putrefaction is the chief stage and first step to generation. Now putrefaction is

<margin>The cause of putrefaction is a moist heat,</margin> occasioned by a moist heat. For a continual moist heat causes putrefaction and changes all natural things from their first form and essence, as well as their virtues and efficacy, into something else. <margin>The power and nature of putrefaction.</margin> For just as putrefaction in the stomach changes and reduces all food <note>original: "meats"</note> into dung, so also putrefaction outside the stomach in a glass vessel changes all things from one form into another: from one essence into another, from one color into another, from one smell into another, from one virtue into another, from one power into another, from one property into another, and generally from one quality into another. 

For it is evident, and proved by daily experience, that many good things which are wholesome and medicinal become, after putrefaction, worthless <note>original: "naught"</note>, unwholesome, and mere poison. So, on the contrary, there are many bad, unwholesome, poisonous, and harmful things which after their putrefaction become good, lose all their unwholesomeness, and become wonderfully medicinal. This is because putrefaction produces great results, of which we have a most famous example in the holy Gospel, where Christ says:

> *Unless a grain of wheat is cast into the earth and putrefies, it cannot bring forth fruit a hundredfold.* <note>A reference to John 12:24, illustrating the idea that death or decay is a prerequisite for new life.</note>

Hence we must also know that many things are multiplied in putrefaction so as to bring forth excellent fruit. <margin>What putrefaction is.</margin> For putrefaction is the change and death of all things, and the destruction of the first essence of all natural things; from this arises a regeneration and a new generation a thousand times better, etc.

<margin>The artificial hatching of chickens.</margin>
You have an example of this in eggs, which contain a mucilaginous fluid <note>original: "humour"</note>. Indeed, any person may ripen an egg in their armpit and hatch a chick just as well as the hen.

<margin>Bringing a dead bird back to life.</margin>
And here we must take notice of something even greater and more significant than this: namely, if that living chick is placed in a glass vessel like a gourd and sealed up, then burnt to powder or ashes in the third degree of heat <note>Alchemy categorized heat into "degrees"; the third degree is a strong, intense heat.</note>, and afterward, while still sealed inside, is putrefied with the most thorough putrefaction of horse dung into a mucilaginous phlegm, then 그 phlegm may be brought to maturity and become a renewed and newly made chick. This occurs if that phlegm is again enclosed in its former shell or container. This is to revive the dead through regeneration and purification <note>original: "clarification"</note>, which is indeed a great and profound miracle of Nature. <margin>The artificial creation of man.</margin>
We must also know that in this manner, men may be generated without a natural father or mother—that is, not from a woman in a natural way. Rather, by the art and industry of a skillful <term>Alchymist</term> <note>original: Alchymist; a practitioner of alchemy, the precursor to modern chemistry, often concerned with the transformation of matter and the creation of life.</note>, a man may be born and grow, as shall be shown later.

<margin>The creation of men from beasts.</margin>
<margin>As the seed is, so is the fruit.</margin>
It is also possible that men may be born of beasts according to natural causes, yet this cannot be done without great impiety and heresy. Specifically, if a man should couple with a beast, and that beast should—as a woman does—receive the <term>Sperm</term> <note>original: Sperm; here used in the sense of reproductive seed.</note> of the man with desire and lust into her <term>matrix</term> <note>original: matrix; the womb or uterus.</note> and conceive, then the sperm necessarily putrefies. Through the continual heat of the body, a man and not a beast is produced from it. For the fruit that is brought forth is always according to the seed that is sown; unless it were so, it would be contrary to the light of Nature and to philosophy. Therefore, just as the seed is, so is the herb that springs from it. Thus, from the seed of an onion, an onion is produced—not a rose, nor a nut, nor a lettuce. So from corn <note>original: Corne; in this period, "corn" referred to any cereal grain like wheat or rye.</note>, corn is produced; from barley, barley; from oats, oats; and so it is with all other fruits which have seed and are sown, etc.

Therefore, they rarely die without the hand of the executioner, or at least carry some mark made by him.

<margin>The artificial creation of humans.</margin>
But we must by no means forget the creation of artificial humans. For there is some truth in this matter, although it has been kept secret for a long time. There have been significant doubts and questions raised by some of the ancient philosophers as to whether it was possible for Nature or Art to beget a human outside of the body of a woman and a natural womb <note>original: matrix</note>. To this I answer that it is in no way contrary <note>original: repugnant</note> to the <term>Art of Alchemy</term> or to Nature; indeed, it is very possible. To achieve it, we must proceed in this way:

Let the <term>semen</term> <note>original: sperm</note> of a man be allowed to decay <note>original: putrefied</note> by itself in a sealed glass flask <note>original: gourd glass; a cucurbit used in distillation</note> for forty days at the highest degree of heat found in horse manure, until it begins to live, move, and stir, which can easily be observed. <margin>How the Philosophical Tree is made.</margin>
The process is as follows. Let gold be calcined with *aqua regia* <note>original: *Aqua Regis*; "royal water," a powerful mixture of acids capable of dissolving gold</note> until it becomes a kind of powder <note>original: chalke</note>. Put this into a gourd-shaped glass vessel <note>original: gourd glasse</note> and pour fresh *aqua regia* over it so that it covers the powder to the depth of four fingers. Then, distill the liquid off again using the third degree of heat <note>the third of four traditional levels of alchemical fire, usually signifying a strong heat such as a hot sand bath</note> until no more vapor rises. Pour the water that was distilled off back onto the gold, then distill it off once more. Do this repeatedly until you see the gold begin to rise in the glass and grow in the manner of a tree, having many boughs and leaves. Thus, a wonderful and pleasant shrub is made of gold, which the alchemists call their "golden herb" and the "Philosophers' Tree." In the same way, you may proceed with silver and other metals, though their calcination must be performed in a different manner using a different *aqua fortis* <note>original: *Aqua fortis*; "strong water," or nitric acid</note>, which I leave to your own experimentation. If you are skilled in alchemy, you shall not go wrong in these matters.

<margin>To make an artificial stone of any form.</margin>

To do this, place the flint into a glass vessel and pour river water over it until the glass is filled. This water is then to be distilled off until not a drop remains. The stone is then dried, the glass is filled again with this water, and it is distilled off once more. This process should be repeated until the glass is entirely filled with this stone.

### Of the Preservation of Natural Things.

<margin>Death is the enemy of things.</margin>
<margin>A contrariety is found in all things.</margin>
Truly, nobody can. Therefore, it is necessary to know one's enemy, for there are many kinds of enemies. It is just as necessary to know evil things as it is to know good things; for who can know what is good without knowing what is evil? Truly, no one can. Similarly, no man who was never sick can know what a blessing health is. Who knows what joy is, if they have never been heavy-hearted or sad? And who can rightly understand what God is, if they know nothing of the Devil? 

Therefore, just as God made known to us the enemy of our soul—namely <note>original: "viz."; an abbreviation for the Latin *videlicet*, meaning "namely" or "that is to say"</note> the Devil—he also revealed to us the enemy of our life: Death. Death is the enemy of our body and our health, as well as the enemy of medicinal and all natural things. He also made known to us how and by what means it may be avoided. For just as there is no disease for which a remedy has not been created and found to cure and expel it, so there is always one thing ordained against another: one water against another, one stone against another, one mineral against another, one poison against another, and one metal against another. There are many more such examples, though it is not necessary to list them all here.

Now, regarding how and by what means everything is to be preserved and kept from harm, we must know that many things are to be preserved in the earth. Specifically, all roots can remain in the earth for a long time without losing their potency <note>original: "vertue"; the inherent power or medicinal quality of the substance</note> or becoming corrupted. In the same way, herbs, flowers, and all fruits stay uncorrupted and green in water. There are also many fruits and apples that can be preserved in water, safe from all kinds of decay <note>original: "putrefaction"</note>, until the new harvest arrives.

<margin>How to preserve flesh and blood.</margin>
In the same way, flesh and blood—which indeed decay <note>original: "putrefied"</note> and quickly become foul-smelling—can be preserved in cold spring water. Not only that, but by adding new and fresh spring water, they may be turned into a <term>quintessence</term> <note>the "fifth essence" or purest, most concentrated part of a substance</note> and be forever preserved from decay and bad odors without using any balsam. This does not only preserve the flesh and blood of dead things, but also of the living. Therefore, a person's body may be preserved from all types of decay and various diseases that result from decay, even better than with common <term>Mummy</term> <note>original: "Mummie"; a medicinal preparation made from embalmed or dried human remains, believed to have healing properties</note>. Now, so that blood may be preserved on its own from decay and stench—not as a quintessence, but in a way that preserves the blood of the living (as we just mentioned)—you must follow this process.

<margin>How the secret remedy <note>original: Arcanum</note> of human blood is to be prepared.</margin>
Let the blood be separated from its <term>phlegm</term> <note>original: "flegm"; here referring to the clear, watery serum of the blood</note>, which separates naturally and rises to the top. Pour this water gently out of the vessel, and in its place put an equal amount of the "water of the salt of blood," which we teach how to make in our <term>Surgery</term> <note>original: "Chirurgerie"; likely referring to the author's medical treatise on wounds</note>. That water immediately mixes with the blood and preserves it so that it will never decay or become foul-smelling, but will remain as fresh and bright red for many years as it was on the first day. This is indeed a great wonder. But if you do not know how to make this water, or do not have it ready, then pour over it an equal amount of the best and most excellent balsam, and this will achieve the same result. Now, this blood is the "balsam of balsams" and is called the *Arcanum of blood* <note>original: "Arcanum"; a deep secret or powerful medical mystery</note>. It is so wonderful and of such great virtue that it is incredible to speak of; therefore, you shall keep it a great secret in <term>medicine</term> <note>original: "Physick"</note>.

<margin>How metals may be preserved. What the enemies of metals are.</margin>
In the preservation of metals, their enemies must first be known so that the metals may be better protected from harm. The primary enemies of metals are all sharp, corroding waters <note>likely strong acids like nitric or sulfuric acid</note>, all corrosive substances, all salts, raw sulfur, antimony, and mercury. To understand specifically how they show their hostility, consider this: sharp waters, corrosive substances, and salts show their enmity by "mortifying" <note>original: "mortifie"; in alchemy, to strip a metal of its external form or metallic luster</note>, dissolving, <term>calcining</term> <note>reducing a metal to a powder through heat or chemical action</note>, and corrupting metals until they are reduced to nothing.

<margin>How the fumes of sulfur discolor metals.</margin>
Raw sulfur shows its enmity through its fumes; for by its fumes, it strips copper of its color and redness, making it white. From white metals—such as silver, tin, lead, and iron—it takes away their whiteness and makes them red or yellowish. From gold, it takes away 그 beautiful, pleasant yellowness and golden color, making it black and so foul that nothing could be more repulsive.

<margin>How antimony spoils and discolors metals.</margin>
Antimony shows its enmity in this way: it spoils, carries away, and preys upon all metals with which it is melted or mixed. Also, not unlike sulfur, its fumes strip metals of their true and natural color and replace it with another.

<margin>Quicksilver destroys metals, and how.</margin>
Quicksilver <note>mercury</note> destroys metals for this reason: it enters into the metals with which it is joined and dissolves them, creating an <term>amalgam</term> <note>original: Amalgama; a blend of mercury with another metal</note>. Therefore, its fumes (which we call common <term>mercury</term>) make all metals brittle so that they cannot be <term>malleated</term> <note>hammered or shaped into sheets</note> and <term>calcines</term> them. It also gives all red metals a golden color...

<margin>How the loadstone may be ruined.</margin>
Any loadstone that mercury has merely touched, or which has been smeared with mercurial oil, or even just placed into mercury, will never attract iron again. No one should wonder at this, for there is a natural cause for it: mercury extracts the *spirit* of iron that was hidden in the loadstone. It is this *spirit* that draws the *spirit* of iron to itself. This principle exists not only in the loadstone but in all other natural things: a foreign *spirit* in a body that is not of the same *nature* as itself always draws to itself a body that is of the same *nature*. We must know this to be true not only of the loadstone, but also of all other natural things, such as *minerals, stones, herbs, roots, humans, and animals* <note>original: "brutes"</note>.

<margin>The natural antipathy between metals themselves.</margin>
Metals have a natural enmity and hatred for one another, as you see in *lead*, which is naturally a very great enemy to *gold*. It breaks apart all the components of *gold*; it makes it foul and weak, spoiling and destroying it even "to death" <note>in alchemy, "death" refers to the loss of a metal's essential metallic qualities or luster</note> more than any other metal.

*Tin* also hates and is an enemy to all metals; it makes them base, brittle <term>immalleable</term>, hard, and useless if it is mixed with them in the fire or during melting.

Regarding metals, you must next know their preservatives, which keep them from all manner of harm or corruption, and also strengthen their nature and power <note>original: "vertue"</note> and intensify <note>original: "exalt"</note> their color.

<margin>Gold is preserved in the urine of young boys.</margin>
First, therefore, concerning gold, you must know that it cannot be preserved better or more beautifully than in the urine of young boys in which sal ammoniac <note>original: "Salt Armoniack"; ammonium chloride, used in metallurgy as a flux and cleaning agent</note> is dissolved, or in a solution of sal ammoniac alone. In these liquids, over time, the color is so highly intensified that it can be heightened no further.

<margin>How silver is preserved.</margin>
<margin>How iron and steel may be preserved.</margin>
<margin>How copper is preserved.</margin>
Silver cannot be better preserved than by being boiled in common water or vinegar in which tartar <note>potassium bitartrate, a byproduct of winemaking</note> or salt has been dissolved. In this way, any old silver that has turned black or dirty is restored by being boiled in these liquids. The best preservative for iron and steel is the lard of a castrated boar <note>original: "Barrow-hog"</note> that has not been salted; this indeed protects iron and steel from rust if they are thinly coated <note>original: "fineered over"</note> with it once every month. Also, if iron is melted with "fixed" arsenic <note>arsenic processed so that it remains solid at high temperatures rather than vaporizing</note>, it will be so renewed and stabilized that, like silver, it will never develop rust. Copper may be preserved if it is only mixed with sublimed mercury <note>mercury that has been vaporized and then re-solidified into a powder</note> or smeared with oil of salt <note>concentrated hydrochloric acid</note>; in this way, it will never again be covered with verdigris <note>the green pigment or crust that forms on copper through oxidation</note>.

<margin>How lead is preserved.</margin>
Lead can be preserved in no better way than in cold earth and in a moist place, according to its natural properties.

<margin>How the loadstone is preserved.</margin>
The loadstone <note>a naturally magnetic mineral</note> is best preserved with iron and steel filings; by this means, it is never weakened but is strengthened daily.

Not only two sorts, but three, four, five, and more may be kept this way if oil is simply put between them. For they are separated by the oil as if by a wall, which will not allow them to be joined together and united; for oil and water are two contraries, and neither can be mixed with the other. Just as the oil will not allow the waters to be united, so on the contrary, the water will not allow the oils to be mixed.

<margin>How all sorts of wood may be preserved.</margin>
Also, all types of wood—whether in houses, bridges, ships, or wherever they may be—can be preserved so that they will never rot <note>original: "putrefied"</note>, whether in water, underwater, out of water in the earth, under the earth, or above the earth. It does not matter if they are placed in the rain, wind, air, snow, or ice, in winter or summer. Furthermore, they will not become worm-eaten, nor will any worms breed in them once they are cut. Now, this preservative is a great <term>secret</term> <note>original: "Arcanum"</note> against all kinds of decay; indeed, it is so excellent a secret that none may be compared to it. And it is nothing else but:

<margin>Fixed oil of sulfur.</margin>
Oil of sulfur, the process for which is this: Let common yellow sulfur be powdered and put into a gourd glass <note>A gourd-shaped flask used in distillation</note>, over which should be poured enough of the strongest <term>nitric acid</term> <note>original: "Aqua fortis"</note> to cover it by three fingers' breadth. Then draw it off by distillation three or four times, and finally until it is dry. Let the sulfur that remains in the bottom—being of a dark, deep red color <note>original: "black, sad red colour"</note>—be put upon marble or in a glass, and it will easily dissolve into an oil. This is a great secret in preserving wood from decay and worms. For this oil so stains <note>original: "tinge"</note> the wood that is anointed with it that it can never be washed out again. Many more things may be preserved with this oil of sulfur from decay, such as ropes and cords in ships, masts, carts, fishing nets, and traps <note>original: "gins"</note> which fowlers and hunters use, and similar items which are often used in water or rain and are otherwise easily rotted and broken. This also applies to linen clothes and many other such things.

<margin>Which liquids are drinkable <note>original: "potable"</note>, and how they are preserved.</margin>
Also, you must know how drinkable liquids are to be preserved, by which we mean wine, beer, mead, vinegar, and milk. <margin>How wine is preserved by sulfur.</margin>
Wine is preserved chiefly by sulfur and the oil of sulfur, by which all wine may be preserved for a long time, so that it remains neither thick nor changed in any other way.

<margin>Beer is preserved with oil of cloves.</margin>
Beer is preserved with oil of cloves, if a few drops of it are put into it—two or three drops for every gallon—or, what is better, with the oil of the root of *Avens* <note>A common woodland herb, *Geum urbanum*, also known as herb bennet, traditionally used to flavor and preserve ale</note>, which prevents beer from souring.

<margin>Mead is preserved with oil of sugar.</margin>
Mead is preserved with oil of sugar, which must be used in the same way as the oil of cloves mentioned above.

<margin>How vinegar is preserved.</margin>
Vinegar is preserved with oil of ginger, which must be used in the same way as the oil of cloves mentioned above.

<margin>How milk is preserved.</margin>
Milk is preserved with oil of almonds made by pressing <note>original: "expression"</note>, which must be used in the same way as the oil of cloves mentioned above.

<margin>Cheese is preserved with St. John’s wort.</margin>
Cheese is preserved from worms with *St. John’s wort*. For if the herb only touches the cheese, no worms will breed in it.

<margin>What the difference is between the Spirit and the Body.</margin>
For what is the body without a spirit? It is nothing at all. Therefore, the spirit—not the body—secretly contains the virtue <note>In this context, "virtue" refers to the inherent power or medicinal property of a substance.</note> and power of the thing. <margin>The Spirit never dies.</margin>
While the body may be destroyed and corrupted in several ways, the spirit cannot. For the living spirit remains forever; it is the subject of life and preserves the body while it is alive. But upon the ruin of the body, the spirit is separated from it, leaving behind a dead body, and returns to the place from which it came—namely <note>original: "viz." <margin>The classification of spirits according to the variety of bodies.</margin>
For there are spirits that are celestial, infernal, human, metallic, and mineral; spirits of salts, of gems, of <term>marcasites</term> <note>A term formerly used for various minerals with a metallic luster, such as pyrite.</note>, of arsenics, of drinkable <note>original: "potable"</note> things, of roots, of juices, of flesh, of blood, of bones, and so on.

<margin>What the life of man is.</margin>
The life of all people is therefore nothing other than an <term>astral balsam</term> <note>A spiritual life force believed to be derived from the stars.</note>, a <term>balsamic impression</term>, a celestial invisible fire, an enclosed air, and a <term>tingeing spirit of salt</term> <note>In alchemy, the "spirit of salt" was an essence of preservation and transformation.</note>. <margin>What the life of metals is.</margin>
The life of metals is a <term>secret fatness</term> <note>Alchemists used "fatness" to describe the oily, combustible, or fusible quality of a substance.</note> which they have received from <term>sulfur</term> <note>In the "Tria Prima" of alchemy, sulfur represents the principle of combustion and soul.</note>. Unless that were in it, no metal could melt <note>original: "flowe"</note>, as we see in iron and steel, which have less sulfur and fatness than all the other metals. Therefore, they are of a drier nature than all the rest.

<margin>What the life of mercury is. Mercury is like a garment made of skins.</margin>
The life of mercury <note>Also known as quicksilver.</note> is nothing other than internal heat and external coldness—that is <note>original: "i. e." (id est)</note>, it makes the internal part of its body hot and the outward part cold. Therefore, it might well be compared to a garment made of skins <note>A fur coat or cloak.</note>, which acts just like mercury to provide both heat and cold. For if a person wears such a garment, it makes them warm and protects them from the cold; but if the smooth side of those skins is placed against the naked body, it makes the person cold and is good against too much heat. For this reason, it was a custom in ancient times—and still is in some places—to wear skins in both summer and winter: as a protection against cold in the one, so against heat in the other. In summer, they turn the smooth side inward and the hairy side outward; and in winter, the hairy side inward and—

The life of flints is a mucilaginous <note>Thick, glue-like, or slimy.</note> matter.

<margin>What the life of marcasites is.</margin>
The life of <term>marcasites</term> <note>Iron sulfide minerals often mistaken for ores.</note>, <term>cachymia</term> <note>An old term for mineral ores that were not quite considered true metals.</note>, talc, cobalt, <term>zimri</term> <note>An archaic term for a specific mineral or metal byproduct.</note>, <term>garnet</term> <note>original: "Granata"</note>, bismuth <note>original: "Wismat"</note>, and of antimony is a <term>tingeing</term> metallic spirit.

<margin>The life of arsenics.</margin>
The life of arsenics, <term>auripigment</term> <note>Orpiment; a deep yellow arsenic sulfide mineral.</note>, orpiment <note>original: "Operment"</note>, realgar <note>A red arsenic sulfide mineral.</note>, and such similar matters, is a mineral and <term>coagulated</term> <note>Solidified or thickened.</note> poison.

<margin>The life of excrements.</margin>
The life of excrements—that is <note>original: "i.e." (id est)</note>, of human dung or animal dung—is their stinking smell; for once this is lost, they are dead.

<margin>The life of aromatic things.</margin>
The life of aromatic things—namely <note>original: "viz." (videlicet)</note>, of musk, <term>ambergris</term> <note>original: "Amber Gryse"; a waxy substance produced by sperm whales.</note>, <term>civet</term> <note>A musky perfume ingredient obtained from the civet cat.</note>, and whatever yields a strong, good, and sweet smell—is nothing other than that pleasant <note>original: "gratefull"</note> odor; for if they lose this, they are dead and of no use.

<margin>The life of sweet things.</margin>
The life of sweet things—such as *sugar*, *honey*, *manna*, *cassia*, and the like—lies in their coloring power <note>original: "tinging"</note> and delicate sweetness. For if that sweetness is taken from them by distilling or subliming <note>The process of heating a substance to turn it into vapor, which then cools back into a solid.</note>, they are dead, useless, and worth nothing.

<margin>The life of resins <note>original: "rozzen"</note>.</margin>
The life of all *resins*, such as *amber*, *turpentine*, and *gum*, is the thick, shiny oiliness <note>original: "muciliginous shining fatnesse"</note> which gives them all their excellent varnish. For when they no longer yield varnish and lose their shine, they are dead.

<margin>The life of plants.</margin>
The life of *herbs*, *roots*, *apples*, and other similar fruits is nothing other than the moisture <note>original: "liquor"</note> of the earth, which they lose naturally if they simply lack water and soil.

<margin>The life of wood.</margin>
The life of *wood* is a certain *resin*; for any wood that lacks *resin* can live no longer.

<margin>The life of bones.</margin>
The life of *bones* is the <term>liquor of mummy</term> <note>In alchemy and early medicine, "mummy" (mummia) was a vitalizing substance believed to be found in the human body or ancient remains.</note>.

<margin>The life of flesh.</margin>
The life of *flesh* and *blood* is nothing else but the <term>spirit of salt</term> <note>Here referring to the preservative property of salt; in chemistry, this later became a name for hydrochloric acid.</note>, which preserves them from smelling and rotting. By itself, it is like water when separated from them.

<margin>The life of every element.</margin>
Now concerning the life of the *elements*, you must know that the life of *water* is its flow. For when it is frozen into ice by the coldness of the *sky* <note>original: "firmament"</note>, it is dead, and its danger <note>original: "mischievousnesse"</note> is taken from it, so that no one can be drowned in it.

<margin>What the life of fire is.</margin>
The life of *fire* is *air*, for *air* makes fire burn with greater intensity and heat. Also, there comes forth from all *fire* a kind of *air* which will blow out a candle and push up a feather, as you may see daily before your eyes. Therefore...

### THE FIFTH BOOK.

#### *Of the Death, or ruin of all things.*

<margin>What Death is</margin>
The death of all natural things is nothing more than an alteration and destruction of their powers and virtues <note>original: "vertues"; in alchemy, "virtues" refers to the inherent medicinal or spiritual properties of a substance</note>, a predominance of that which is evil <note>In this context, "evil" refers to corruption, decay, or the loss of a substance's vital essence</note>, and an overcoming of what is good. It is an abolishing of the former nature and the creation <note>original: "generation"</note> of a new and different nature. For you must know that there are many things that, while they are alive, possess several virtues, but when they are dead, they retain little or nothing of...

However, so that I do not seem to write according to my own opinion only, but from my experience, it is necessary that I produce one example with which I shall silence those sophisters <note>original: "Sophisters"; here referring to academic or theoretical philosophers who oppose alchemical practice</note> who say that we can receive nothing from dead things, nor should we seek or expect to find anything in them. Let every faithful alchemist and physician spend their whole lives searching into these three <note>referring to the three primary alchemical principles: salt, sulfur, and mercury</note>. For they will abundantly reward him for all his labor, study, and costs.

<margin>What the death of man is.</margin>
But to come to particulars, and to write specifically of the death and destruction of every natural thing—what the death of every thing is, and in what manner every thing is destroyed—you must first know that the death of man is, without doubt, nothing other than an end of his daily work. It is the taking away of the air, the decaying of the **natural balsam** <note>original: "Naturall balsome"; in Paracelsian medicine, this was the internal preservative or life-force that kept the body from decaying</note>, the extinguishing of the **natural light** <note>original: "naturall light"; the "Lumen Naturae," or the innate wisdom and divine spark within the natural world</note>, and the great separation of the three substances—namely, the body, soul, and spirit—and their return to from where they came. Because a natural man is made of the earth, the earth is also his mother, into which he must return and there lose his natural earthly flesh. In this way, he will be regenerated at the Last Day in a new celestial and purified flesh, as Christ said to **Nicodemus** when he came to him by night. These words of regeneration must be understood in this manner.

<margin>What the destruction of metals is.</margin>
The death and destruction of metals is the disjoining of their bodies and their **sulfurous fatness** <note>original: "sulphureous fatnesse"; an alchemical term for the combustible, oily principle within minerals</note>. This may be done in several ways, such as by **calcination**, **reverberation**, **dissolution**, **cementation**, and **sublimation**. 

<margin>The calcination of metals is diverse.</margin>
But the calcination of metals is not of only one sort. One is made with salt, another with sulfur, another with **strong water** <note>original: "Aqua fortis"; nitric acid</note>, another with common **sublimate** <note>mercury(II) chloride, a corrosive white powder used in chemical reactions</note>, and another with **quicksilver** <note>mercury</note>.

Calcination with sublimed mercury <note>referring to mercuric chloride, a corrosive white powder</note> is this: the metal is made into thin plates, and the mercury is put into an earthen vessel that is narrow toward the top and wide at the bottom. Then, let it be set into a gentle fire made with coals, which must be blown a little until the mercury begins to fume and a white cloud goes forth from the mouth of the vessel. Then, let the plate of the metal be put into the top of the vessel; in this way, the sublimed mercury will penetrate the metal and make it as brittle as a piece of coal.

<margin>Calcination with quicksilver.</margin>
Calcination with quicksilver <note>liquid mercury</note> is when the metal is made very small and thin and is **amalgamated** with quicksilver. Afterward, the quicksilver is strained through leather, and the metal remains in the leather like chalk or sand.
