<margin>A twofold preparation of Saffron of Mars <note>original: "Crocus Martis"</note>.</margin>
But let us proceed to show how metals may be yet further mortified <note>original: "mortified"; in alchemy, the process of destroying a metal's external form or metallic state, usually by turning it into a powder</note>. First, regarding iron: know that it is mortified and reduced into a powdered oxide <note>original: "Crocus"</note> in this way. Hammer steel into very thin plates. Heat these plates until they are red hot, then quench them in the best wine vinegar. Do this repeatedly until the vinegar has acquired a significant redness. Then, distill off the vinegar until nothing remains but a dry powder. This is a most excellent Saffron of Mars <note>original: "Crocus Martis"; a reddish-brown iron oxide used in medicine and alchemy</note>.

There is also another way of making Saffron of Mars which partly exceeds the previous method and is made with far less cost and effort, as follows:

Strew sulfur and tartar <note>original: "Tartar"; potassium bitartrate, a byproduct of winemaking</note> in equal quantities upon the plates of steel. Then, **reverberate** <note>original: "reverberate"; to heat in a furnace where the flames are reflected or "reverberated" onto the material</note> them. This will produce a most excellent powdered oxide, which must then be scraped off from the plates.

You must also know that every plate of iron or steel, if it is dissolved <note>original: "melted"</note> with strong water <note>original: "Aqua fortis"; nitric acid</note>, will also make a very fine powdered oxide. It is also made with oil of vitriol <note>original: "oyle of Vitriall"; sulfuric acid</note>, spirit of salt <note>original: "spirit of Salt"; hydrochloric acid</note>, alum water, the water of sal ammoniac <note>original: "Salt Armoniacke"; ammonium chloride</note>, and of saltpeter <note>original: "Salt Nitre"; potassium nitrate</note>, as well as with sublimed mercury <note>mercuric chloride, a corrosive substance</note>. All of these mortify iron and turn it into a powdered oxide; however, none of these latter methods are to be compared to the first two, for they are only used in alchemy and not at all in medicine <note>original: "Physicke"</note>. Therefore, for medical use, employ only the first two methods and ignore the rest.

<margin>The mortification of copper.</margin>
The mortification <note>original: "mortification"; in alchemy, the process of destroying a metal's external form or metallic state, usually by turning it into a powder, salt, or oxide</note> of copper—namely, so that it may be reduced into vitriol <note>original: "Vitriall"; copper sulfate, often appearing as blue or green crystals</note> or verdigris—can be done in many ways. There are many processes for it, yet one is far better than another, and one more profitable than another. Therefore, it is most convenient here to record the best and most profitable methods and to remain silent about the rest. The best, easiest, and most exact way of reducing copper into vitriol is this:

<margin>The vitriol of copper is made in two ways.</margin>
Let plates of copper be dipped in **spirit of salt** <note>hydrochloric acid</note> or **saltpeter** <note>potassium nitrate</note>, and let them be hung in the air until they begin to turn green—which will indeed happen quickly. Wash off this greenness with clear spring water, dry the plates with a cloth, and wet them again with the spirit of salt and saltpeter. Repeat this until the water is visibly green or much vitriol swims on the top. Then pour away the water or evaporate it, and you have a most excellent vitriol for medicine. In alchemy, there is no fairer, more excellent, or better vitriol than what is made by **strong water** <note>original: "Aqua fortis"; nitric acid</note>, **royal water** <note>original: "Aqua regis"; a mixture of nitric and hydrochloric acids</note>, or **spirit of sal ammoniac** <note>ammonium chloride solution</note>. The process is this:

Let plates of copper be dissolved <note>original: "melted"; in this context, it refers to chemical dissolution in acid rather than thermal melting</note> with one of the aforementioned waters. As soon as the greenness is extracted and the plates are dried, let the greenness be taken off with a hare's foot or in some other way as you please, just as **ceruse** <note>white lead pigment</note> is taken off from plates of lead. Let them be wetted again as before until the plates are wholly consumed; by this means, a most glorious vitriol is made, such that you cannot help but wonder at it.

For as the matter is, so are the colors that are produced, although for the most part they flow from the blackness of the "dead earth" <note>original: *caput mortuum*, the solid residue left after distillation or heating</note>. For you who are skillful in <term>alchemy</term> see that the dead earth of <term>aqua fortis</term> <note>original: *Aquafortis*; literally "strong water," referring to nitric acid</note> comes out black from the fire; and the more ingredients there are in it, the more various the colors show themselves in the air. For in the death of all natural things, other colors are seen which change from the first color into others, each one according to its nature and property.

<margin>The preparation of verdigris to be used in alchemy.</margin>
Now we will speak of the <term>verdigris</term> <note>a green pigment or crust formed on copper</note> which is to be used in alchemy. Its preparation and process is this:

Make very thin plates of copper and strew upon them salt, sulfur, and <term>tartar</term> <note>potassium bitartrate, a sediment from wine casks</note>, ground and mixed together in equal quantities, inside a large <term>calcining pot</term> <note>a ceramic vessel used for heating substances to high temperatures</note>. Then <term>reverberate</term> <note>heat in a furnace that reflects heat onto the material</note> them for twenty-four hours with a strong fire, but ensure the plates of copper do not melt. Then take them out, break the pot, and place the plates (with the material that sticks to them) into the open air for a few days. The material upon the plates will be turned into a beautiful verdigris. <margin>How to make a sweet precipitate.</margin>
Moreover, you must take notice of a great secret concerning precipitated <term>Mercury</term>, namely <note>original: viz.</note> if after it is colored, it is sweetened <note>original: dulcified</note> with the water of the salt of <term>Tartar</term> <note>potassium carbonate</note> by pouring the water upon it and distilling it off repeatedly. <margin>And the use of it.</margin>

Although much labor and sweat are required for this precipitate, it will sufficiently repay you for your effort and costs. It will yield more profit than can be gained by any art or trade whatsoever. <margin>How the sulfur and the vitriol of gold are made.</margin>
Take two or three pounds of pure <term>gold</term>, which you should beat into thin plates. When you have enough of the <term>vitriol of gold</term>, boil it well in distilled rainwater, always stirring it with a spatula. Then the <term>sulfur of the gold</term> is driven up to the surface <note>original: "superficies"</note> of the water like fat, which you should skim off with a spoon. Do the same with more <term>vitriol</term>. Now, after all the <term>sulfur</term> is taken off, evaporate that rainwater until it is all dry, and the <term>vitriol of gold</term> will remain at the bottom, which you may easily dissolve by itself upon a marble slab in a moist place. <margin>The mortification and fixation of sulfur.</margin>
Take common yellow sulfur, finely powdered, and draw from it by distillation <term>strong water</term> <note>original: *Aqua fortis*; nitric acid</note> that is very sharp. Do this three times. Then <term>sweeten</term> <note>original: dulcifie; to wash or neutralize until the acid or salt is removed</note> the sulfur, which will be black and at the bottom of the vessel, with distilled water until the water comes away sweet and the sulfur no longer smells. Then process this sulfur in a closed <term>reverberatory furnace</term> <note>a furnace that reflects heat back onto the substance</note> just as you would do with antimony. It will first turn white, then yellow, and finally as red as <term>cinnabar</term> <note>a bright red mineral, mercury sulfide</note>. When it reaches this state, you may rejoice, for it is the beginning of your riches. This processed sulfur <term>tinctures</term> <note>original: tingeth; to transform the color or essence of a metal</note> silver into the most excellent gold and restores the human body to perfect health. This processed and <term>fixed</term> <note>chemically stabilized so it no longer evaporates</note> sulfur has more power than is lawful to speak of.

<margin>The mortification of salts.</margin>
The mortification of all salts, and anything salty, consists of removing and distilling away their wateriness, oiliness, and their spirit. If these are taken away, the remains are afterwards called the "dead earth" or <term>death’s head</term> <note>original: *Caput Mortuum*; the useless residue left after distillation or sublimation</note>.

The mortification of pearls is to calcine them and dissolve them in sharp vinegar until they take the form of milk.

<margin>The mortification of the loadstone.</margin>
The mortification of the <term>loadstone</term> <note>a naturally magnetized mineral</note> is to anoint it with the oil of mercury or to put it into <term>quicksilver</term> <note>liquid mercury</note>; afterward, it will no longer attract iron at all.

<margin>The mortification of flints and stones.</margin>
The mortification of flints and stones is to calcine them.

<margin>The mortification of marcasites.</margin>
The mortification of <term>marcasites</term> <note>iron pyrite or similar metallic ores</note>, <term>cachymas</term> <note>a term for mineral or metallic dross</note>, talc, cobalt, zinri, granuti, zunitter, bismuth <note>original: Unifmut</note>, and...

# *Of the Resurrection of Natural things.*

<margin>
The raising again of natural things.
</margin>
**T**HE Resurrection and renewing of natural things is not a minor matter, but a profound and great secret in the nature of things; it is more divine and angelic than it is human and natural.

I desire to be understood here with great distinction, and in no other way than my opinion stands—as Nature daily and clearly shows, and experience confirms—lest I should be exposed to the lies <note>The text cuts off here at the end of the page; the author likely intends to warn against the false accusations of those who misunderstand his spiritual or alchemical theories.</note>

<summary>This page introduces Book Six, focusing on the "resurrection" or restoration of natural things to their former state or a higher form, describing it as a profound secret of nature that borders on the divine.</summary>
<keywords>resurrection, alchemy, renewal, Paracelsus, natural philosophy, divine secrets</keywords>

--- Page 234 ---
<meta>This page continues the author's defense against his critics and clarifies his distinction between natural death (which only God can reverse) and "mortification" (alchemical death), which man can potentially reverse through art and faith.</meta>

<page-num>52</page-num>
<header>Of the Nature of things. BOOK VI.</header>

...and slanders of charlatans <note>original: "Mountebanks"—dishonest people who sell ineffective medicines or lie about their skills</note>, my enemies (who interpret everything I do in the worst possible way), as if I would usurp divine power and attribute this to Nature, which she was never able to perform. Therefore, we must cautiously consider that there is

<margin>Death is twofold.</margin>
a twofold death: namely <note>original: "viz." (videlicet)</note>, violent and voluntary. One can be raised again, while the other cannot. Therefore, do not believe those false reasoners <note>original: "Sophisters"—those who use clever but fallacious arguments</note> who say that a thing once dead or mortified <note>term: "mortification"—in alchemy, the state of a substance being "killed" or broken down so it can be transformed</note> can never be raised again, and who give no credit to the resuscitation and restoration of things. This error of theirs is quite significant. Indeed, it is true that whatever dies or perishes by a natural death—and whatever Nature mortifies because of her predestination—God alone can raise again, or it must necessarily be done by His command. Thus, whatever Nature destroys, man cannot restore.

<margin>What things may be raised again.</margin>
But whatever man destroys, he can restore again, and once restored, he can spoil it again. Man has no further power of his own, and if he should attempt to do anything more, he would claim God’s power for himself. Yet, he would labor in vain and be confounded unless God assisted him, or he had so much faith as to remove mountains. Even to such a man, this is possible, and greater things than this. Because the Scripture says, and Christ himself spoke it:

> If you have faith as a grain of mustard seed, and say to this mountain, "Go and be moved there," it shall be moved; all things will be possible for you, and nothing impossible. <note>A reference to Matthew 17:20.</note>

## Lib. VI. Of the Nature of Things.

<margin>What things cannot be raised again.</margin>
Which of these may be raised again is to be understood in this way: whatever dies naturally has its end by predestination, as the will and decree of God permits. Yet it also happens that death occurs through various diseases and different accidents <note>original: "casualties"</note>, and these can never be raised again; neither is there any preservative to be used against predestination and the natural term of life. But that which is mortified <term>mortification: in alchemy, the process of "killing" a substance to change its form, rather than its final natural death</term> may be both raised again and revived, which may be proved by various arguments that we shall set down at the end of this book.

<margin>It is one thing to die, and another thing to be mortified.</margin>
Therefore, there is a great difference between dying and being mortified, and they must not be taken for one and the same thing under the same name. Even in practice, they are very different. For consider a man who dies a natural and predestined death: what further good or profit is there in him? Nothing; he is only cast into the earth for worms. For he is a stinking carcass and belongs to the earth.

But the same is not to be understood of a man who is slain with a sword or dies by some similar violent death. For his whole body is useful and good, and may be prepared into a most precious mummy <note>In early modern medicine, "mummy" (mumia) was a substance derived from human remains, believed to contain life-preserving properties</note>. For although the spirit of life departed from such a body, the balsam <note>original: "balsome"—the vital essence or fluid believed to sustain life and prevent decay</note> in which the life resides remains, which indeed acts as a balm to preserve other men's bodies.

So you may see in metals: when a metal is about to die, it begins to be overcome with rust, and as much of it as is thus overcome is dead. When all the metal is devoured with rust, it is entirely dead, and such rust can never be reduced back into true metal again,

<margin>What the ashes of metals are.</margin>
The *ashes* are *volatile* and cannot be brought back into a *metal*, but only into *glass* and *dross*. But the *calx* of *metals* is *fixed* and may be brought back into its own *metal*.

<margin>What the calx of metals is.</margin>

From this it follows that the *salt* must be extracted out of the *ashes* of *metals* so that they cannot be brought back into a *metal*; then they are perfectly *volatile*. This difference and this point should be especially noted, for much depends upon it.

<margin>The resuscitation of metals is twofold.</margin>
But to set aside examples and move on to the <term>praxis</term> <note>original: "Praxis"; the practical application or exercise of a branch of learning</note> of resurrection and restoration, it is necessary and most convenient to begin with metals, because metallic bodies often resemble human bodies.

<margin>Reducing metals into quicksilver.</margin>
We must know, therefore, that the resurrection and restoration of metals is twofold. One type reduces <term>calcined</term> <note>original: "calcined"; burned or heated to a powder</note> metals back into their first metallic body; the other reduces metals into their "first matter"—that is, into <term>quicksilver</term> <note>original: "Quicksilver"; mercury</note>.

The process of the latter is this: <term>calcine</term> a metal with common quicksilver, put this <term>calx</term> <note>original: "Calx"; the powdery remains left after a metal has been burned or oxidized</note> and an equal amount of quicksilver into a <term>sublimatory</term> <note>original: "Sublimatory"; a vessel used for sublimation, where a solid is heated into a gas and then condensed back into a solid</note>, and let them stand until both are thickened into an <term>amalgam</term> <note>original: "Amalgama"; a blend of mercury with another metal</note>. #### *Of the Transmutation of Natural things.*

<margin>What Calcination is and what its types are.</margin>
The first degree, therefore, is <term>Calcination</term> <note>original: "Calcination"; the process of heating a substance to high temperatures, typically in air, to change its physical or chemical state, such as reducing it to ash or powder</note>, which also includes <term>Reverberation</term> <note>original: "Reverberation"; a method of heating in a furnace where the flame is deflected (reverberated) down onto the material</note> and <term>Cementation</term> <note>original: "Cementation"; a process of heating a solid in a bed of powder to alter its properties without melting it</note>. There is very little difference between these when it comes to the matter of calcination; therefore, it is the most important degree here. By reverberation and cementation, many physical things are calcined and reduced to ashes, especially metals. Once a substance is calcined, it is not reverberated or cemented any further.

**Sublimation** is the second degree, and one of the most important for the **transmutation** of many natural things. Within it are included **exaltation**, **elevation**, and **fixation**. It is quite similar to **distillation**. For just as in distillation, water rises from all phlegmatic <note>original: "flegmatick"; here referring to watery or moist substances</note> and liquid things and is separated from its physical mass, so in sublimation, that which is spiritual is raised from what is physical <note>original: "corporeall"</note>. Besides sublimation, many beneficial properties <note>original: "vertues"</note> and wonderful things are discovered in minerals. Many things are made "fixed" and become stable <note>original: "constant"</note> so they can withstand the fire, and this is done in the following manner:

<margin>Rules concerning **Sal Ammoniac**.</margin>

<margin>What **Solution** is, and its types.</margin>
The third degree is **solution**, under which are to be understood **dissolution** and **resolution**. This degree most commonly follows sublimation and distillation; specifically, it is the process by which the matter remaining at the bottom is resolved <note>dissolved into a liquid state</note>.

Now solution is of two types: one of cold and the other of heat; the one without fire and the other in fire.

A cold dissolution dissolves all salts, all corrosive things, and all <term>calcined</term> <note>original: "calcined"; substances reduced to a dry powder by heat</note> things. Whatever is of a salty and corrosive quality is dissolved by it into oil, liquor, or water. This takes place in a moist, cold cellar, or else in the air on a marble slab or in a glass vessel. For whatever is dissolved in the cold contains an "airy spirit of salt," which it often acquires and assumes during sublimation or distillation. And whatever is dissolved in the cold or in the air may again be solidified into powder or a stone by the heat of the fire.

<margin>What substances a hot solution dissolves.</margin>
But a hot <term>solution</term> <note>the process of dissolving a solid into a liquid using heat</note> dissolves all fat and sulfurous <note>original: "sulphureous"</note> substances. Furthermore, whatever the heat of the fire dissolves, coldness congeals into a solid mass.

<margin>Two types of solution: heat and cold.</margin>
Whatever heat solidifies <note>original: "coagulates"</note> is dissolved again by cold or by the air. We must also recognize that whatever the air or the cellar dissolves is of a very great dryness and has a secret, corrosive fire hidden within it. Conversely, whatever is dissolved in fire, or by its heat, possesses a sweetish coldness <note>original: "frigidity"</note> once removed from the fire. This is the only way that <term>solution</term> is to be understood.

<margin>The nature and types of putrefaction.</margin>
<term>Putrefaction</term> <note>in alchemy, this refers to the decomposition or "death" of a substance, which is necessary for its rebirth and transformation into a higher state</note> is the fourth degree, which includes <term>digestion</term> <note>the slow, gentle heating of a substance</note> and <term>circulation</term> <note>the continuous distillation of a liquid where it rises as vapor and falls back as liquid</note>.

Now, putrefaction is one of the primary degrees. Indeed, it might deservedly have been the first of all, were it not against the true order and <term>mystery</term> <note>original: "mystery"; the secret spiritual and chemical process of alchemy</note> hidden here and known to only a few. For these degrees must follow one another like links in a chain or steps on a ladder, as has already been said.

<margin>The established order of degrees must be followed when creating tinctures.</margin>
If one of the links were taken away, the chain would be broken and the "prisoners" <note>a metaphor for the volatile spirits or substances being contained within the vessel</note> would go free and escape. Similarly, if one step of a ladder were removed from the middle and placed at the top or bottom, the ladder would be broken. Many people would fall headlong from it, risking their bodies and lives.

Therefore, you must understand that these degrees must follow one another in the correct order. Otherwise, the entire work of our mystery would be ruined, and our labor and efforts would be in vain and fruitless.

<margin>The power of putrefaction.</margin>
Now <term>putrefaction</term> <note>in alchemy, the process of decomposition or "death" that allows a substance to be reborn in a higher state</note> has such power that it destroys the old nature and brings in a new one. All living things are killed in it, all dead things are decomposed in it, and all dead things recover life in it.

Putrefaction removes from all corrosive spirits the sharpness of the salt and makes them mild and sweet; it changes their colors and separates the pure from the impure, placing the pure above and the impure beneath.

<margin>What distillation is and its types.</margin>
Distillation is the first stage toward the <term>transmutation</term> <note>the alchemical conversion of one substance into another</note> of all natural things. Under it are included <term>ascension</term> <note>the rising of vapors</note>, <term>lavation</term> <note>washing or purification</note>, and <term>fixation</term> <note>the process of making a volatile substance stable and resistant to fire</note>.

Through distillation, all waters, liquids, and oils are refined <note>original: "subtilized"</note>. From all fatty substances, oil is extracted; from all liquids, water; and from all <term>phlegmatic</term> <note>watery or moisture-heavy</note> substances, water and oil are separated.

<margin>Cohobation. Fixation by distillation.</margin>
In addition, many things are <term>fixed</term> in distillation by <term>cohobation</term> <note>the repeated redistillation of a liquid back onto its own solid residue to concentrate its properties</note>, especially if the substances to be fixed contain water within them, as <term>vitriol</term> <note>a metallic sulfate, usually of iron or copper</note> does. If vitriol is fixed, it is called *<term>colcothar</term>* <note>a reddish iron oxide residue remaining after the distillation of vitriol</note>.

<term>Alum</term> <note>a mineral salt used as an astringent</note>, if it is fixed with its own water, is called the "sugar of alum." This is also resolved into a liquid which, if it is putrefied for a month, produces a water with the sweetness of sugar. This is of great power and is an excellent secret in <term>medicine</term> <note>original: "physick"</note> for cooling any metallic heat <note>likely referring to fever or inflammatory conditions caused by an imbalance of minerals</note> in man, as we have written about more extensively in our book *Of Metallic Diseases*.

And as you have heard of **vitriol** <note>original: "Vitriall"; metal sulfates like copper or iron sulfate</note> and **alum** <note>original: "Allum"; a mineral salt used in dyeing and medicine</note>, so also **saltpeter** <note>original: "Salt nitre"; potassium nitrate</note> and other **watery minerals** may be fixed <note>made stable and resistant to heat</note> by **cohobation**.

<margin>What cohobation is.</margin>
Now **cohobation** <note>the process of repeatedly re-distilling a liquid from its own solid residue</note> is when the **residue** <note>original: "dead head" or *caput mortuum*; the solid remains left after distillation</note> is frequently soaked with its own distilled water, and that water is then drawn off again by **distillation**.

<margin>The power of distillation in the transmutation of things.</margin>
Moreover, in **distillation**, many bitter, harsh, and sharp things become as sweet as **honey**, **sugar**, or **manna** <note>a sweet plant secretion used as a mild laxative or food</note>. On the contrary, many sweet things—such as sugar, honey, or manna—may be made as harsh as **oil of vitriol** <note>concentrated sulfuric acid</note> or **vinegar**, or as bitter as **gall** <note>bile</note> or **gentian** <note>a bitter medicinal root</note>, or as sharp <note>original: "Eager"; from the French *aigre*, meaning sour or sharp</note> as a **corrosive** acid.

Many **waste products** <note>original: "Excrementitious things"</note> lose their great stench through **distillation**, as the smell actually passes out into the water.

Many **aromatic** things lose their pleasant scent.

And just as **sublimation** <note>the process of turning a solid directly into vapor and back to solid</note> alters the quality and nature of things, so also does **distillation**.

<margin>What coagulation is, and its types.</margin>
**Coagulation** <note>the process of a liquid becoming a solid or semi-solid</note> is the stable <note>original: "fixt"</note> state. Now there is a twofold **coagulation**: one by cold and the other by heat—that is <note>original: "i. e."</note>, one by **air** and the other by **fire**. Each of these, in turn, is twofold, so that there are four sorts of coagulations: two of cold and two of fire.

The coagulations produced by fire are permanent <note>original: "fixed"</note>, but the others produced by cold are not.

One type is produced only by common **air**, or without **fire**. The other is produced by the higher **heavens** <note>original: "Firmament"</note> of the **winter stars**, all of which coagulate waters into **snow** and **ice**.

But the **coagulation** <note>the process of turning a liquid or soft substance into a solid</note> of fire, which is the only type to be noted here, is produced by the artificial and gradual fire of the alchemists, and it is fixed and permanent. For whatever such a fire solidifies remains in that state.

The other kind of **coagulation** is performed by the **Etnean** <note>original: "Ætnean"; referring to volcanic or subterranean heat, named after the volcano Mount Etna</note> and mineral fire within mountains. This is governed by the **Archeus** <term>Archeus</term> <note>In Paracelsian alchemy, the "Archeus" is the internal life-force or "inner chemist" that directs the growth and formation of all things in nature</note> of the Earth, which regulates the heat much like an alchemist does. Whatever is solidified by such a fire is also fixed and constant—as you see in minerals and metals. These actually begin as a **mucilaginous** <note>jelly-like or slimy</note> matter and are solidified into metals, stones, flints, salts, and other bodies by the volcanic fire in the mountains, through the work of the **Archeus** of the Earth and the operator of Nature.

<margin>What things cannot be solidified.</margin>
We must also know that fire cannot solidify any water or moisture, but only the **liquors** and **juices** of all natural things.

Furthermore, no **phlegm** <note>original: "flegm"; a watery, inactive distillate produced during chemical processes</note> can be solidified unless it was originally a solid <note>original: "corporeall"</note> matter, to which it may return through the industry of a skillful alchemist.

Similarly, any jelly-like matter or **spermatic** <note>seed-like or generative</note> sliminess may be solidified into a body and solid matter by the heat of fire, but it can never be turned back into water.

And just as you have heard concerning **coagulation**, you should also know regarding **solution** <note>the process of dissolving a solid into a liquid</note>: no solid matter can be dissolved into water unless it was water at its beginning—and this is true of all minerals.

<margin>What a Tincture is and its various kinds.</margin>
**Tincture** <note>In alchemy, a tincture is a potent substance or "essence" capable of transforming the physical properties of another material</note> is the seventh and last degree, which concludes the entire work of our mystery for **transmutation** <term>transmutation</term> <note>the conversion of one substance into another, most famously base metals into gold</note>. It makes all imperfect things perfect, transforming them into a most excellent essence and into a state of perfect health, and changing them into another color.

*Tincture, therefore, is a most excellent matter with which mineral and human bodies are colored. Through it, they are changed into a better and more noble essence, reaching the highest possible perfection and purity.*

For a tincture colors all things according to its own nature and color.

<margin>All things that are to be colored must be in a liquid state.</margin>
Now, there are many types of tinctures—not only for metallic bodies but for human bodies as well. This is because anything that penetrates another matter, or colors it with a different hue or essence so that it no longer resembles its former self, may be called a tincture.

Therefore, there are many and various sorts of tinctures: namely, those for metals, minerals, human bodies, waters, liquids, oils, salts, all fatty substances, and indeed all things that can be brought to a **flux** <term>flux</term> <note>a state of being melted, fluid, or flowing, usually through the application of heat</note>, whether outside of the fire or within it.

For if a tincture is to "tinge" (or color) a substance, it is necessary that the body or matter being treated is "opened" and remains in a state of flux. Unless this is the case, the tincture cannot operate. It would be as if someone were to throw **saffron** <note>a spice often used in alchemy as a pigment due to its deep yellow-orange color</note> or any other dye upon frozen water or ice; it would not color the ice as quickly as it would if it were thrown into liquid water. And even if it did color the ice, it would simultaneously melt the ice back into water.

<margin>The transmutation of metals into silver and gold.</margin>
However, for the five lesser and more impure metals—namely mercury (☿), tin (♃), lead (♄), iron (♂), and copper (♀)—to be transmuted into the greater, purest, and most perfect metals, namely gold (☉) and silver (☽), it cannot be done without the <term>Tincture</term> <note>a potent alchemical substance capable of "staining" or transforming the quality of a metal</note> or the <term>Philosophers' Stone</term>.

Now, since we have previously revealed the secrets of Tinctures in the seven degrees and described them there, it is unnecessary <note>The original text likely omitted "not" here: "it is [not] necessary"</note> to spend any further effort on this topic. Instead, be satisfied with those things which we have written in other books concerning the transmutations of metals.

<margin>The transmutation of iron into copper.</margin>
Now, there are other transmutations of imperfect and impure metals, such as the transmutation of iron (♂) into copper (♀), which may be done in various ways.

One way is if plates of iron are boiled in water of <term>Vitriol</term> <note>original: "Vitriall"; a term for sulfate minerals or sulfuric acid</note>, or are <term>cemented</term> <note>heated while surrounded by a powdered substance to alter the metal's surface</note> with <term>calcined</term> <note>burned to a powder</note> vitriol, or if the iron is heated red-hot and then quenched in oil of vitriol.

By these three methods, iron may be transmuted into very good and heavy copper, which indeed melts <note>original: "flows"</note> well and weighs as much as any natural copper.

<margin>The transmutation of iron into lead.</margin>
Plates of iron may also be, as it were, reduced and transmuted into lead, so that the metal becomes as soft as natural lead, though it does not melt as easily. The process is this:

Take filings of iron (♂) and an equal amount of powdered <term>Borax</term> <note>a mineral salt used as a flux to help metals melt</note>, mix them well together, and put them in a...

Cement and melt them as described above; in this way, all the blackness and darkness will be removed from the lead, and it will be as white as fine English tin.

<margin>The kind of separation to be discussed here.</margin>
But so that you may briefly understand the reason for our purpose in this eighth book, you must know that we do not intend to treat here the elements of all natural things. We have already sufficiently discussed those secrets <note>original: "Arcana"</note> in the *Archidoxis* <note>one of Paracelsus's major works on the "primary teaching" of medicine and alchemy</note> regarding the separation of natural things. Through that separation, every one of them is set apart and distinctly divided, both materially and substantially. That is to say <note>original: "viz."</note>, we see how two, three, four, or more things are mixed into one body, and yet only a single substance is visible. It often happens that the physical matter of that thing cannot be known by anyone, or identified by any specific name, until a separation is performed. Then, sometimes two, three, four, five, or more things emerge from that one matter, as is shown by daily experience in the **Art of Alchemy.**

<margin>The nature of Electrum.</margin>
For example, consider *Electrum* <note>In alchemy, "Electrum" often refers to a natural or artificial alloy of the seven metals, rather than just gold and silver</note>. <margin>The definition of separation.</margin>

I am speaking of the separation of the three principles—such as Mercury, Sulphur, and Salt <note>In Paracelsian philosophy, these are the "tria prima," the three basic components of all matter</note>—and the extraction of the pure from the impure, or the pure, excellent spirit and quintessence <note>the most essential or "fifth" element of a substance</note> from a

<margin>The various kinds of separation.</margin>
Now, there are many kinds of separation, many of which are unknown to us. Those that we have experienced regarding elementary, dissolvable natural things shall be described here according to their types.

<margin>The separation of the microcosm.</margin>

<margin>The human body is twofold after death.</margin>

One of these ascends on high like an eagle; the other falls downward to the earth like lead.

<margin>The nature of the elementary body.</margin>
The elementary body decays, is consumed, and becomes a rotting, stinking carcass. Once buried in the earth, it never comes forth or appears again.

<margin>The nature of a sacramental body.</margin>
But the sacramental body—that is <note>original: "i.e."</note>, the sidereal <note>relating to the stars or spirit-body</note> or celestial body—never decays or is buried, nor does it occupy any physical space. This body appears to people and is seen even after death.

*From this come ghosts, visions, and supernatural apparitions.*

Therefore, he who boasts that he is able to separate all natural things in this manner must necessarily have long experience and perfect knowledge of all natural things.

Moreover, he must be a skillful and well-practiced <term>Alchemist</term>, so that he may know what is combustible and what is not; what is fixed <note>original: "fixt"; referring to substances that do not evaporate or change when heated</note> and what is not; what will flow and what will not; and which things are heavier than others. Also, he must be experienced in the natural color, smell, acidity, harshness, sourness, bitterness, sweetness, and the degree, <term>temperament</term> <note>original: "complexion"; the inherent nature or balance of qualities in a substance</note>, and quality of every thing.

<margin>The degrees of Separation: What and how many there are.</margin>
Also, he must know the degrees of Separation, such as **Distillation**, **Resolution**, **Putrefaction**, **Extraction**, **Calcination**, **Reverberation**, **Sublimation**, **Reduction**, **Coagulation**, **Powdering**, and **Washing**.

<margin>What distillation separates.</margin>
By **Distillation**, Water and Oil are separated from all physical things.

<margin>What resolution separates.</margin>
By **Resolution** <note>the process of dissolving or reducing a substance into its parts</note>, metals are separated from minerals, one metal is separated from another, Salt is separated from the other Principles, and fat (and that which is light) is separated from that which is heavy.

<margin>Putrefaction.</margin>
By **Putrefaction**, fat is separated from lean, pure from impure, and the decayed from the undecayed.

<margin>Extraction.</margin>
By **Extraction**, pure is separated from impure, the spirit and <term>quintessence</term> <note>the purest or most concentrated essence of a substance</note> are separated from the body, and the thin is separated from the thick.

<margin>Calcination:</margin>
By <term>Calcination</term> <note>the process of heating a substance to high temperatures in air to change its physical or chemical state</note> is separated watery moisture, fat, natural heat, odor, and whatever else is combustible.

<margin>Reverberation.</margin>
By <term>Reverberation</term> <note>heating a substance in a furnace where the flame is reflected or "reverberated" down onto it</note> is separated color, odor, what is combustible, all humidity, wateriness, fat, and whatsoever is unstable <note>original: "inconstant"</note>, or fluid <note>original: "fluxil"; meaning easily melted or flowing</note> in any thing, etc.

<margin>Sublimation.</margin>
By <term>Sublimation</term> <note>heating a substance until it turns into vapor and then solidifies again upon cooling, often used to purify</note> is separated the fixed <note>substances that resist the fire and do not evaporate</note> from the volatile, the spiritual from the physical <note>original: "corporeall"</note>, the pure from the impure, <term>Sulfur</term> from <term>Salt</term>, <term>Mercury</term> from <term>Salt</term>, etc.

<margin>Reduction.</margin>
By <term>Reduction</term> <note>the process of restoring a substance, such as a metal oxide, back to its metallic state</note> is separated what is fluid <note>original: "fluxil"</note> from what is solid, a metal from its mineral ore, one metal from another, a metal from its waste <note>original: "drosse"</note>, and fat from what is not fat.

<margin>Coagulation.</margin>
By <term>Coagulation</term> <note>the process of thickening or solidifying a liquid</note> is separated wateriness from humidity, and water from Earth.

<margin>Powdering.</margin>
By **Powdering** are separated powder, sand, ashes, and <term>calx</term> <note>the powdery oxide left after a metal has been burned or calcined</note>; mineral, vegetable, and animal substances are separated one from the other; and all powders which are of an unequal weight are separated by winnowing, as chaff is separated from grain <note>original: "corne"</note>.

<margin>Washing.</margin>
By **Washing** are separated ashes and sand, a mineral from its metal, that which is heavy from what is light, vegetable and animal matter from what is mineral, Sulfur from Mercury and Salt, and Salt from Mercury.

<margin>The Preparation of Metal is manifold.</margin>
But passing by the theory, we will now begin the practice and come to particulars.

You must therefore note that the separation of metals is the first by right, and we shall therefore treat of it according to this method and manner.

# Of the Separation of Metals
## *from their Ores.* <note>original: Mines</note>

<margin>By fluxing powders.</margin>
The separation of metals from their ores is done in various ways: specifically, by boiling and melting with fluxing powders, such as alkali salt, litharge <note>a mineral form of lead carbon monoxide used in refining</note>, fluxing salt, glass dross <note>waste material from glass making used as a flux</note>, rock salt <note>original: Salt Gemme</note>, saltpeter <note>potassium nitrate</note>, and so on. Let them be put in a crucible and melted in a furnace. In this way, the metal, or <term>regulus</term> <note>the pure metallic mass that settles at the bottom of a crucible during smelting</note>, will fall to the bottom of the crucible, while the other matter will float on top and become waste <note>original: droffe; the stony or earthy material separated from metals during smelting</note>. You shall boil this metallic regulus in a <term>reverberating furnace</term> <note>a furnace that reflects heat from the roof down onto the material being treated</note> until all the metal becomes pure and freed from all its waste. By this means, the metal is well "digested" and, so to speak, refined from all its dross.

Many times one ore contains more than one metal—such as copper and silver, copper and gold, lead and silver, or tin and silver. You shall know this if the metallic regulus is dissolved in the correct manner after being heated in a melting pot. For within it, all base <note>original: imperfect</note> metals are separated—such as iron, copper, tin, and lead. If a double quantity of lead is added to the regulus, those base metals all evaporate <note>original: goe into a fume</note>, and only fine silver or gold is left behind in the pot.

<margin>By <term>Aqua Fortis</term>.</margin> <note>literally "strong water"; a historical name for nitric acid</note>

...the other. If two metals, or one of them, are dissolved <note>original: resolved</note>, the other will fall to the bottom like sand and be precipitated; in this manner, they are separated. Metals may also be separated by melting <note>original: flowing</note> through the following process: melt the metals, and when they are in flux, cast <margin>By sulfur <note>original: Sulphur</note>.</margin> into them the best flour of sulfur <note>original: flower of Sulphur; a fine powder produced by sublimation</note> you can get—namely <note>original: viz.</note>, an ounce to every pound of the metal. In this manner, other metals besides gold and silver may also be treated—including copper, iron, tin, and lead—as well as whatever substances are prepared from them. These include red <term>electrum</term> <note>an alloy of gold and silver, often containing copper</note>, white magnesia, <term>aurichalcum</term> <note>a golden-colored brass alloy</note>, calcined lead, <term>latten</term> <note>original: Laton; a brass-like alloy</note>, brass from cauldrons, and whatever metals of this kind are transmuted. These can be processed with mercury, provided they are first powdered and separated from any foreign <note>original: heterogeneous</note> matter. For the nature and condition of mercury is this: it will unite and amalgamate with metals, yet it joins with one sooner than another, depending on whether the metal has a greater or lesser affinity for it.

# Of the Nature of Things
## BOOK 8 <note>original: LIB. VIII.</note>

In this consideration, fine **Gold** is the most important, then fine **Silver**, then **Lead**, then **Tin**, then **Copper**, and lastly **Iron**.

So amongst transmuted metals, the first is "part with part" <note>an alloy of equal parts</note>, then **ash**-colored **lead**, then **latten** <note>original: Laton; a brass-like alloy of copper and zinc</note>, then **cauldron brass**, then red, and finally the newest white. By this means, nothing but the **quicksilver** will pass through the **leather** or **cloth**. The metal which it attracted remains in the leather or cloth like <term>calx</term> <note>a powdery metallic residue or oxide</note>, which you may afterwards reduce into a metallic body by melting it with **alkali salt** <note>original: salt Alcali</note> or some other salt.

By this process with **mercury**, all metals may—after <term>calcination</term> <note>heating a substance to a high temperature to reduce it to powder</note> and powdering—be extracted and separated from one another by a skillful and industrious **alchemist**.

In the same manner, and quite easily, **tin** and **lead** may be separated from **copper** (or **copper** vessels) and from **iron** and **steel** coated with **tin** without any fire or water, using the **amalgam** of **quicksilver** alone.

Also, **beaten gold**, **leaf gold**, or **silver**—as well as any other metal beaten or ground—that has been used for writing or applied with a <term>pencil</term> <note>original: pencill; here meaning a fine artist's brush</note> or quill upon cloth, parchment, paper, leather, wood, stone, or anything else, may be dissolved <note>original: resolved</note> by **quicksilver**. The **quicksilver** may then be separated from those metals once again.

<margin>Using corrosive waters.</margin>
Now, the separation of metals in <term>Aqua fortis</term> <note>literally "strong water"; nitric acid</note>, <term>Aqua Regis</term> <note>literally "royal water"; a mixture of nitric and hydrochloric acids</note>, and similar corrosive waters, is done in this manner.

Take a metal that is mixed and joined with another, and beat it into thin plates or grind it into powder. Put it into a separating vessel and pour as much common *Aqua fortis* over it as is necessary. Let them stand and be <term>macerated</term> <note>soaked or softened</note> until all the metal is <term>resolved</term> <note>dissolved</note> into a clear liquid. If it is silver containing any gold, all the silver will be dissolved into the water, and the gold will also be <term>calcined</term> <note>reduced to a powder by heat or chemical action</note> and settle at the bottom like black sand. In this manner, gold and silver are separated. Now, if you wish to separate the silver from the *Aqua fortis* without distillation, put a plate of copper into the water, and the silver will immediately settle at the bottom of the liquid like snow, while the copper plate will begin to be consumed little by little.

The separation of silver and copper by common *Aqua fortis* is done in this way: Let the copper which contains silver, or the silver which contains copper, be reduced to thin plates or powder and put into a glass vessel. Pour as much common *Aqua fortis* as is sufficient over it. By this means, the silver will be calcined and settle to the bottom like white chalk, but the copper will be dissolved and turned into a clear liquid. If this liquid, along with the dissolved copper, is separated from the silver <term>calx</term> <note>powdery residue</note> by a glass funnel into another glass, then the copper dissolved in the water may be so <term>precipitated</term> <note>original: precipiated; to cause a substance to settle out of a solution</note> with common water, rainwater, or any other water, that it will settle to the bottom of the glass like sand.

Now, the separation of hidden gold from any metal...

Moreover, through the use of <term>cement</term> <note>a dry, powdered chemical mixture used to refine metals by heating them in layers</note> and the process of reverberation, two metals mixed together may be separated from one another. However, the silver is consumed by the cement and thus extracted from the fine gold. In the same way, copper is separated from silver, iron and tin are separated from copper, and iron or lead are separated from tin, and so forth.

## *Of the Separation of Minerals.*

After having explained—as we have done so far—the separation of metals from their earth and matter, as well as the separation of one metal from another, and having covered this as briefly as possible, it is now necessary to discuss those things from which metals grow and are generated. These include the three principles—Mercury, Sulphur, and Salt—as well as all minerals in which the **first being** of metals (that is, the spirit of metals) is found. 

This is evident in **marcasites, garnets, <term>cachymiae</term>** <note>original: Cachymiies; a Paracelsian term for minerals that are considered "imperfect" or transitional stages of metallic growth</note>, **red talc,** the **<term>Azure stone</term>** <note>Lapis Lazuli</note>, and similar substances, in which the first being of **Gold** is found through the process of <term>sublimation</term> <note>the process of heating a substance until it turns into vapor and then solidifies again</note>.

Similarly, the first being of **Silver** is found in **white marcasite, white talc, <term>orpiment</term>** <note>original: Auripigmentum; a yellow arsenic sulfide mineral</note>, **arsenic, <term>litharge</term>** <note>lead monoxide, often a byproduct of silver refining</note>, and so on.

The first being of **Iron** is found in **cobalt, <term>zinc ores</term>** <note>original: Zinetus; likely referring to calamine or other zinc-bearing minerals known to miners at the time</note>, etc. 

The first being of **Copper** is found in **zinc ores, vitriol, verdigris,** etc. 

The first being of **Tin** is found in **zinc ores, bismuth,** etc. 

The first being of **Lead** is found in **antimony, <term>minium</term>** <note>red lead</note>, etc. 

The first being of **Mercury** <note>original: Quicksilver</note> is found in **cinnabar.**

Regarding this "first beginning," you must know that it is a volatile spirit, still existing in a state of volatility, just as an infant lies in the womb of its **Mother**, which...

## Of the Separation of Vegetables.

<margin>How plants are separated.</margin>
**T**he separation of those things which grow out of the Earth and are combustible—such as fruits, herbs, flowers, leaves, grass, roots, woods, etc.—is performed in many ways.

For first, by distillation, the phlegm <note>original: Flegm; in this context, the watery part of a substance's essence</note> is separated from them, then the mercury <note>the "spirit" or volatile principle in the alchemical system of the three primes</note>, then the oil, then the resin <note>original: Re-fine; likely an archaic spelling or OCR error for resin</note>, then the sulfur <note>the "soul" or combustible principle</note>, and lastly the salt <note>the solid, earthy base remaining after combustion</note>.

When all these separations are made according to the <term>Spagyric Art</term> <note>a method of medicine based on the alchemical principle of "solve et coagula"—to dissolve and recombine</note>, many notable and excellent medicines are produced, which are to be used both internally and externally.

But now, seeing that idleness is so much in demand among physicians, and all labor and study has turned only to arrogance, I truly do not wonder that such preparations are everywhere neglected. Coal is sold at such a low price because of this neglect; indeed, if blacksmiths could do without coal for forging and working their metals as easily as physicians do in preparing their medicines, coal miners <note>original: Colliers</note> would have been reduced to extreme poverty long ago.

<margin>A criticism of physicians.</margin>
In the meantime, I will give the <term>Spagyric physicians</term> their due praise. For they are not given to idleness and sloth, nor do they walk about in proud attire or plush and velvet garments, showing off rings on their fingers, wearing swords with silver hilts by their sides, or wearing fine and colorful gloves on their hands. Instead, they diligently follow their labors, sweating through entire nights and days by their furnaces.

<margin>The praise of Chemists, and how they differ from other physicians.</margin>
These do not spend their time outdoors for recreation, but take delight in their laboratory. They wear leather garments with a pouch and an apron with which they wipe their hands. They put their fingers among coals, into clay, and dung, rather than wearing gold rings. They are sooty and black, like blacksmiths or coal miners <note>original: Colliers</note>, and do not pride themselves on clean and beautiful faces. They are not talkative when they visit the sick, nor do they boast of their medicines; for they know well that the craftsman must not praise his work, but the work must praise the craftsman, and that the sick cannot be cured with fine words.

<margin>How many degrees of alchemy there are.</margin>
Therefore, laying aside all these kinds of vanities, they delight to be busy with the fire and to learn the degrees <note>In this context, "degrees" refers to the specific stages, methods, or processes of the alchemical art</note> of the science of alchemy. Of this order are *distillation, resolution* <note>the process of breaking a substance down into its component parts</note>, *putrefaction* <note>controlled fermentation or decomposition used to release the essence of a material</note>, *extraction, calcination* <note>heating a substance to high temperatures to reduce it to ash or powder</note>, *reverberation* <note>heating a material in a furnace where the flame is reflected or "reverberated" back onto the substance</note>, *sublimation* <note>heating a solid until it turns into vapor and then collecting it as it cools back into a solid</note>, *fixation* <note>the process of making a volatile substance stable and resistant to fire</note>, *separation, reduction, coagulation, tincture* <note>the extraction of the medicinal "soul" or color of a substance</note>, etc.

How these separations may be done by the help of distinct degrees according to the art of alchemy has been spoken of in general terms already. Therefore, it is unnecessary to repeat it here.

But to proceed to particulars and briefly explain the practice, you must know that *water, spirit, liquor, oil,* etc., cannot be separated by the same process from flowers, herbs, seeds, leaves, roots, trees, fruits, and woods using the process of distillation.

For herbs require one process, flowers another, seeds another, leaves another, roots another, and trees another.

...another, the stalks another, the fruit another, and woods another.

<margin>The degrees of fire in distillations</margin>
And in this stage of distillation, there are also four distinct degrees of fire <note>In alchemy, "fire" refers to specific levels of heat intensity</note> to be considered.

The first degree of fire in distillation is Mary's Bath <note>original: *Balneum Mariæ*; a water bath or double boiler used for gentle, indirect heating</note>; this distillation is performed in water.

The second degree of fire is distillation performed in ashes.

The third is in sand.

The fourth is in an open <note>original: naked</note> fire. Distillation may also be performed using strong water <note>original: *Aqua fortis*; nitric acid, used as a powerful solvent</note> and other sharp <note>acidic or corrosive</note> waters.

<margin>With what degrees of fire every vegetable is to be distilled.</margin>
To the first degree of fire belong herbs, flowers, seeds, and similar items.

To the second: leaves, fruits, etc.

To the third: roots and boughs of trees, etc.

To the fourth: wood and similar materials.

Note that every one of these must be beaten small and bruised <note>crushed or ground to increase surface area</note> before they are put into the still.

And this concludes what is said concerning the distillation of waters out of vegetable substances.

Regarding the separation and distillation of oils, the process is the same as that of water, except that some of them must be distilled by descent <note>original: *per descensum*; a method of distillation where the heat is applied from above and the essence is drawn downward into a receiver, rather than rising as steam</note> and cannot ascend like waters; the process for these must be changed accordingly.

However, liquors are not separated in distillation like waters or oils, but are squeezed <note>original: expressed</note> from their physical <note>original: corporeall</note> substances with a press.

# On the Monstrous Signs of Men

<margin>Various monstrous signs or marks.</margin>
Many people are born deformed with monstrous marks or signs: for example, one person has an extra finger or toe, while another lacks one. The fingers of some grow together while in the mother's womb. Another has a twisted <note>original: "wry"</note> foot, arm, or neck, etc., and is born with it. Another has a hump on his back. Likewise, hermaphrodites are born—that is, those who are both male and female, possessing the organs of both a man and a woman, or else lacking both. I have observed many of these monstrous signs in both males and females; all of these are to be considered signs of secret, evil <term>ascendants</term> <note>original: "ascendents"; in astrology, the sign of the zodiac rising on the eastern horizon at the moment of birth, believed to influence physical appearance and character</note>. This confirms the proverb: "The more crooked, the more wicked," and "Lame limbs, lame deeds." 

<margin>What monstrous signs indicate.</margin>
For these are signs of vices, and they rarely signify anything good.

Just as an executioner marks his sons with shameful <note>original: "infamous"</note> marks, so do the evil ascendants impress supernatural, harmful marks upon their offspring so that they may be more easily identified and avoided. These offspring show marks on their forehead, cheeks, ears, fingers, hands, eyes, tongues, etc., which may be short or cut. Each of these shameful signs indicates a specific vice. For instance, a mark branded onto a woman's face, or the cutting off of her ears, usually signifies theft. The cutting off of fingers indicates cheating gamblers <note>original: "Dicers"</note>, and the cutting off of a hand—

# *Of the Astral Signs of Physiognomy*
## *in Man.*

<margin>The origin of physiognomy.</margin>
**T**he signs of <term>physiognomy</term> <note>the practice of judging character or fate from physical appearance, especially the face</note> receive their origin from the superior stars. This art of physiognomy was greatly esteemed by our ancestors, and especially by Heathens, Tartars, and Turks, and other peoples among whom it was the custom to sell men as slaves; it is not yet altogether set aside among Christians. Yet, many errors have crept in alongside it, which have not yet been noticed by anyone, while every dull and ignorant fellow takes it upon himself to judge others without any kind of discernment. It is truly remarkable that these errors have never been recognized by observing the actual works, deeds, and abilities of the men themselves.

Now, if anyone should argue against us here, saying that the signs of physiognomy are from the stars, and that the stars have no power to compel any...

<margin>*Stars are of two kinds.*</margin>
To better understand these matters, you must realize that **stars** are of two kinds: **terrestrial** <term>earthly</term> and **celestial** <term>heavenly</term>. The former belong to wisdom, while the latter belong to folly.

And just as there are two worlds—the greater <term>the Macrocosm or universe</term> and the lesser <term>the Microcosm or man</term>—and the greater usually governs the lesser, so too the stars of the **Microcosm** <note>the internal spiritual and intellectual forces within a person</note> can rule over and overcome the **celestial** stars.

<margin>*The purpose of the stars is to serve man, not to command him.*</margin>
**God** did not create the **planets** and other **stars** of the **heavens** to rule over humanity. Instead, like all other creatures, they were meant to obey and serve us. And although the celestial <note>original: "imperiour"</note> stars may influence <note>original: "incline"</note> people and mark them—as well as all other earthly bodies—with natural signs according to the manner of their creation <note>original: "generations"</note>, this is not a form of power or sovereignty. Rather, it is a predestined duty and function designed so that nothing may remain hidden or concealed; instead, an object's inward force and power can be revealed through outward signs.

<margin>What black eyes signify.</margin>
To proceed with the practice of what we intended—that is, to list some of the signs of men and their meanings in part:

You should know that black eyes, besides indicating a healthy constitution, also frequently signify a constant mind—one that is not wavering or fearful, but vigorous, sincere, true, and devoted to virtue.

<margin>What gray eyes signify.</margin>
Gray eyes are a sign of a deceitful and fickle <note>original: "changeable"</note> man.

<margin>Weak eyes.</margin>
Weak eyes signify good judgment, a witty mind, and profound deliberation <note>deep thoughtfulness</note>.

<margin>Purblind <note>partially blind or vision-impaired</note>.</margin>
Purblind eyes—and those that roll upward, downward, and to both sides—signify a false and crafty man who cannot easily be deceived. Such a person is treacherous, hates work, and is lazy, earning his living through slothful means like gambling <note>original: "Dice"</note>, usury <note>lending money at high interest</note>, sexual vice <note>original: "Whoring"</note>, robbery, and so on.

<margin>Small and deep eyes.</margin>
Small and deep-set eyes mostly signify weak and feeble vision, with blindness following in old age. They also indicate men who are strong, warlike, bold, deceitful, nimble, and prone to conflict <note>original: "factious"</note>. While they patiently endure their circumstances, the ends of their lives are usually tragic.

<margin>Great eyes.</margin>
Large eyes signify a greedy and ravenous man, especially if they bulge out from the head.

<margin>Always blinking.</margin>
Eyes that are always blinking <note>original: "winking"</note> indicate weak sight and suggest a man who is fearful and anxious <note>original: "solicitous"</note>.

## Of the Astral Signs of Chiromancy.

Concerning the signs of chiromancy <note>the art of reading character or predicting the future from the lines of the hand</note>, we must maintain that they arise from the superior stars of the seven planets; and we must understand and judge them by those seven planets.

<margin>What chiromancy is.</margin>
Now, chiromancy is an art that does not only look into the hands of men and make judgments by their lines and wrinkles, but also considers all herbs, woods, hard stones, soils <note>original: "earthes"</note>, and rivers—and whatever else has lines, veins, or wrinkles.

Nor is this art free from those errors which previous astronomers were guilty of.

For they assigned the fingers of both hands to the planets and the most important <note>original: "chiefest"</note> stars, even though there are only five fingers on one hand (ten on both), yet the planets are reckoned to be only seven.

How then can these things agree with each other?

Now, if there were seven fingers on each hand, it might then be granted that every finger could be assigned to a different <note>original: "severall"</note> planet.

<margin>Whether the fingers are assigned to the planets.</margin>
But it often happens that some men may have only seven fingers on both hands, the rest being accidentally <note>original: "casually"</note> cut off; but seeing that they were cut off, and...

But if there must be only five fingers on each hand while there are seven planets, and these are mutually compared among themselves, it would then be necessary for the assignments of the planets to be put into a box to decide which two planets must give way and be left out.

Yet because this cannot be, and the planets have neither dice nor lots in the heavens <note>original: "Firmament"</note>, it would be a matter of wonder if anyone should take this power upon himself to assign the fingers by the names of the planets and signs: the thumb to *Venus*, the fore-finger to *Jupiter*, the middle-finger to *Saturn*, the ring-finger to the *Sun*, and the little-finger to *Mercury*—while in the meantime casting out *Mars* and the *Moon*, as if they were excluded from their group <note>original: "tribe and liberty"</note>.

Because things are this way, who can wonder that *Mars* stirs up his followers <note>original: "sons"</note> with righteous indignation to kill that caster of lots, or to bear a perpetual hatred against him? Who can wonder why the Moon should weaken the brain of that player, or take away his reason?

And this is their first error which, as we have said, they have committed in <term>chiromancy</term> <note>the art of reading character or fate from the lines of the hand</note>.

It often happens that the original and natural lines of the hands are changed by injuries and accidents, or are made larger or smaller, or appear in other places.

Just as a highway blocked by an obstruction—whether stopped up by a landslide <note>original: "fall of a mountain"</note> or ruined by a flood—forces people to take a nearby detour, the same thing happens with the old lines of the hands. Sometimes, after wounds or ulcers heal, new lines grow along with new flesh, and the old ones are completely erased <note>original: "abolished"</note>.

In the same way, the lines are defaced by hard labor, or the original lines grow larger. It is like a tree: if a young tree sends out many branches on all sides and these are cut off, the tree itself grows thicker.

But so that we may at last proceed to the practice of the art of <term>chiromancy</term> <note>the art of reading character or destiny from physical lines</note> and briefly state our opinion: I want you to know that I will change nothing regarding the hands, but will accept and be satisfied with the observations and descriptions of the Ancients. However, in this practice of *Chiromancy*, I intend to write about those things which the Ancients did not mention, such as the *Chiromancy* of *Herbs*, *Woods*, *Stones*, and similar things.

But by way of argument, one might object here that no herb is older than another as long as it grows—four or five months at most—if the calculation <note>original: "supputation"</note> begins from May until autumn, at which time herbs die and fall from their root.

<margin>The condition of the herb's spirit.</margin>
To this I answer that from God there is but one power <note>original: "vertue"</note> in a root, which is the "first being" and spirit of the herb. By means of this, the herb grows and is sustained until its predestined time, and until it is elevated to the production of seed. This is a sign and a mark that the power returns to the root, and thus the herb is dried. As long as that spirit—which is the primary power of the herb—remains in the root, the herb is renewed every year, unless that spirit is taken away along with the herb and decays. Then the herb is not renewed, for the root is dead and has no more life remaining in it.

But the manner in which that spirit is taken from the root (along with the herb), or from the earth (along with the root), so that its power cannot return into the root or from the root into the earth, is not to be considered here. For that is a sublime mystery of nature and is not to be openly revealed because of ignorant physicians who not only scoff at but despise such secrets. Therefore, what we have omitted here, we shall set down in our *Herbal*.

Moreover, the younger the herbs are, the more they excel in power and virtue.

<margin>Young herbs must be applied to old diseases, and vice versa.</margin>

Ignorant physicians have never considered this, and through their ignorance, they have destroyed more people than they ever cured.

So the mineral of iron is distinct from that of tin and lead, and so on for the rest.

<margin>By what signs mines are discovered.</margin>
Now, concerning the other signs of the internal earth, as well as the colors of minerals, we shall briefly discuss them as follows:

Whenever miners come across a rich <note>original: "fat"; in early mining, "fat" earth referred to soil dense with mineral oils or salts, indicating high fertility for metal growth</note> earth, which indicates a vein of pure and new metal, that is a very good sign, assuring that the metal forming that vein is not far away.

Similarly, if the earth that is dug up contains no metal but is rich, and of a white, black, green, or blue color, or has a clay-like texture, then that is also a good sign of some valuable metal hidden beneath it. Therefore, you must continue digging and not give up.

Miners first take notice of the most excellent and beautiful colors, such as green earth, or <term>chrysocolla</term> <note>a green copper carbonate mineral</note>, <term>verdigris</term> <note>a bright green pigment or crust formed on copper</note>, azure <note>likely azurite, a blue copper ore</note>, <term>cinnabar</term> <note>the bright red ore of mercury</note>, <term>sandarac</term> <note>here referring to realgar, a red arsenic sulfide</note>, <term>orpiment</term> <note>original: "Auripigmentum"; a deep yellow arsenic ore</note>, and <term>litharge</term> <note>a secondary mineral of lead, often produced during the refining of gold or silver</note> of gold and silver, and so on. Almost every one of these usually signifies a specific metal or mineral.

Thus, verdigris, chrysocolla, and green earth for the most part signify <term>copper</term>.

Similarly, azure, white <term>arsenic</term>, or litharge of silver signify the metal <term>copper</term>.

Likewise, cinnabar and sandarac sometimes signify <term>gold</term>, sometimes <term>silver</term>, and sometimes a mixture of both.

<margin>What flashes of light <note>original: "Coruscations"</note> signify in mines.</margin>
Now, concerning <term>coruscations</term> <note>shimmering lights or "flashes" believed to be seen over mineral-rich ground at night or in the dark of a mine</note>, they must be diligently and studiously observed. Wherever the flash of light reaches, the course of the metal vein extends just as far.

<margin>Flashes of light come in three colors.</margin>
Moreover, you should know that these flashes of light appear in three colors—white, yellow, and red—by which all metals are revealed to us. A white flash signifies white metals, such as tin, lead, or silver; a red flash signifies red metals, such as copper and iron; and a yellow flash signifies golden metals.

<margin>How the Chaldeans and Greeks hid their treasure.</margin>
The ancient *Chaldeans* and *Greeks*, if they feared being driven away or banished during times of war, would hide their treasure and mark the location in a unique way. They would choose a specific day, hour, and minute of the year and observe where the Sun or Moon cast a shadow; they would then bury and hide their treasure in that exact spot.

<margin>What Sciomancy is.</margin>
They call this art <term>Sciomancy</term> <note>original: "Sciomancy," from the Greek *skia* (shadow) and *manteia* (divination)</note>, that is, the Art of Shadowing. Many other arts have been grounded in these shadow-methods; through them, many hidden things have been revealed, and all spirits and astral bodies <note>the celestial or spiritual influences that Paracelsus believed governed the material world</note> are made known.

These are Kabbalistic <note>original: "Cabalisticall"; referring here to secret or mystical knowledge</note> signs that cannot deceive, and therefore they should be carefully noted.

<margin>Divining rods are unreliable.</margin>
Therefore, you must be careful not to let yourself be seduced by the divinations of unreliable arts, for they are vain and fruitless—especially divining rods <note>original: "dowsing rods," sticks used in an attempt to locate water or ores</note>, which have deceived many miners. If they show something truly once, they fail ten times.

Additionally, we must not trust other fraudulent signs from the devil, which appear supernaturally <note>original: "preternaturally"</note> during the night or at inconvenient times, such as ghosts and visions. I would have you know that while the devil can produce and cause signs, he does so only out of pure fraud and deceit.

So it is said that no church is built but that the devil builds his chapel there. No chapel is built but that he sets up his altar. There is no good seed sown but that he sows...

## *Of some peculiar Signs of Natural and Supernatural things.*

<margin>The meaning of a pig, horse, cow, bear, fox, dog, and sheep in the Hebrew language.</margin>
The name of a *pig* signifies a filthy and unclean animal. A *horse* signifies a strong and patient animal. A *cow* signifies a devouring and insatiable beast. A *bear* signifies a strong, victorious, and untamed brute. A *fox* signifies a shifting and crafty beast. A *dog* signifies an animal that is false even to those of his own kind. A *sheep* signifies a mild and profitable beast that is harmful to no one.

Because of this, a man may be called a *pig* because of his sordid and swinish life.

And a *horse* for his endurance <note>original: "bearing"</note>, for which he is eminent.

And a *cow* because she is insatiable with food and drink and knows no limit to her belly.

And a *bear* because he is misshapen and stronger than other men.

A *fox* because he is a turncoat and deceitful, adapting himself to everyone while offending no one.

A *dog* because he is faithful to no one but his own mouth; he is false and unhelpful <note>original: "inofficious"</note> to all.

And a *sheep* because he harms nobody but himself, and is more useful to everyone else than he is to himself, etc.

<margin>The liver is the source of blood.</margin>
And it is no wonder that the liver can show that by natural signs. For the origin of the blood is in the liver, and from there, through the veins, it is spread into the whole body and is thickened <note>original: "coagulated"; here referring to the biological process of blood turning into solid tissue.</note> into flesh.

Therefore, from a diseased and poorly functioning liver, no healthy or fresh blood can be produced, just as from bad blood, no wholesome flesh can be formed.

Furthermore, even without examining the liver, the state of the flesh and blood may be known. For those strange colors signify diseases and ailments.

<margin>What the knots in an infant's navel signify.</margin>

By these, it may be predicted how many children the mother of the infant has already birthed or shall birth in the future.

<margin>The branches of a deer's antlers signify its age.</margin>
The same <term>Signator</term> marks the horns of a <term>Hart</term> <note>A male red deer.</note> with branches, by which its age is known. For as many branches as the horn has, that is how many years old the deer is. And seeing as he grows a new horn every year, the age of the deer may be known up to twenty or thirty years.

<margin>What the circles on a cow's horns represent.</margin>
Similarly, the <term>Signator</term> of a cow marks her horns with circles, by which it may be known how many calves she has brought forth. For every circle signifies one calf.

<margin>The teeth of a horse.</margin>
The same <term>Signator</term> brings forth the first teeth of a horse so that for the first seven years, its age may be known by its teeth. For a horse is first born with fourteen teeth, of which it loses two every year, and so in the span of seven years, it loses them all.

But regarding how those signs and images of the <term>Gamaheaus</term> may be distinguished, and what they signify magically, a great deal of experience and knowledge of the nature of things is required, which cannot be perfectly taught here.

You must take careful note here that a stone, or any <term>Gamaheaus</term>, cannot excel in the property and virtue of more than one star, and thus it is influenced <note>original: "qualified"</note> by only one planet.

And although there may be two or more planets influencing earthly bodies, just as they are joined together in the higher heavens, one is always overpowered by the other. For just as one house cannot tolerate two masters, because one always thrusts out the other, so it is here: one rules, and the other serves. Or, like someone who overcomes the person keeping a house, casts him out by force, and sets himself up as master of the house—disposing of everything according to his pleasure and making the other his servant.

So also one star expels another, one planet another, one <term>Ascendant</term> <note>The astrological sign rising on the eastern horizon at a specific moment, thought to exert a strong influence over an object's nature.</note> another, one influence another, one impression another, and one element another. For just as water quenches fire, so one planet destroys the qualities of another and introduces its own.

This is to be understood in the same manner...
